World.title: As Israel’s military advances its yellow line, Gazans fear they’re being pushed to the sea
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On a Gaza seaside that looks more like a beach resort than a battleground, Palestinians splash in the sun. This crowd is grateful for peaceful pauses in a war that’s dragged into its third summer.

But despite talk of peace negotiations and withdrawals, very few believe it’s over.

“This war has taught me to be afraid of hope,” said Tamer Al-Sheikh. “We’ve hoped a lot through four or five truces, but the conflict continues.”

With only a few pauses, Israeli airstrikes hit Gaza almost daily as Israel says it is targeting wanted Hamas militants.

At the same time, Israeli troops have continued creeping west, expanding their military footprint and squeezing two million Palestinians into an ever smaller area, forcing a scramble for survival toward the Mediterranean Sea.

Under the Gaza peace agreement last October, Israel accepted that it would pull back its troops behind what’s known as the “yellow line,” the edge of Israeli military control inside Gaza. That would amount to less than 50 per cent of the territory along its border. But Israel’s army now controls more than 60 per cent, saying the new boundary is necessary for “operational security”.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he’s told his generals to keep going to 70 per cent.

Earlier this month, he rejected a U.S. plan to phase out both Israeli military and Hamas militant control of Gaza, saying Israel “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.” The militant group has agreed to give up weapons only in tandem with a phased Israeli pullback, leaving a deadlock.

CBC’s visual investigations team has verified the near constant forward movement of Israeli troops and expansion of the yellow line using satellite images. Eyewitness accounts and video captured by freelancers on the ground in Gaza have confirmed the military advances.

The impact on Gaza’s civilians has been profound.

WATCH | How Israel's yellow line is moving: Israel’s yellow line is moving, pushing Palestinians closer to the sea | Duration 7:50 Israel’s military front in Gaza was supposed to remain frozen after a ceasefire deal in October, but as CBC’s Saša Petricic explains, the yellow line is advancing and pushing Palestinians westward toward the Mediterranean Sea.

Blocks move without warning

Palestinians regularly wake up to find the yellow cement markers sitting right next to their homes, nudged metres or hundreds of metres closer overnight. Israeli forces aren’t far behind.

“Suddenly, at 6 a.m. I saw the stones had moved,” said Hala Mustaha, pointing to bright yellow blocks in the middle of Salah al-Din Street in Gaza City. “My neighbours were already moving their things, but I have no idea where I can go.”

A yellow block demarcating what's known as the 'yellow line,' which has separated the Gaza Strip's Israeli-held and Palestinian zones since the October ceasefire, is visible in Jabalia, northern Gaza Strip. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Essam Dawla had to transplant his family four times.

“The tanks came day after day to shoot at us,” he said, describing the days after the yellow blocks appeared. “Then came the Apache helicopters, with bullets flying into our house. You can’t imagine the panic.”

In the north, satellite images show how the yellow line has moved from October to July, with the nearby Halawa tent camp growing more than 20 times larger as displaced Palestinians are pushed here from their previous shelters.

In the camp, Ismail Al-Barsh sits in front of his tent with a grandson on his lap. He lost another grandson when the boy’s classroom was hit by an Israeli airstrike near the yellow line.

He’s afraid the same will happen here.

“Now even Halawa isn’t safe,” Al-Barsh said. “Every day, we see more gunfire, to advance the yellow line, again.”

Residents of Halawa Camp say they hear fighting and worry that the line will force them to displace again. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

More than 1,200 Palestinians have been killed here since the ceasefire started last fall, according to UN figures. That brings the total of Gazans who have died since this conflict started on Oct. 7, 2023 to more than 70,000, a figure compiled by Gaza officials and reportedly accepted by Israel .

‘Defensive measures’ says Israel

Israel insists its movement of the yellow line is consistent with the ceasefire deal.

In a written reply to questions from CBC News, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it is working “to clearly and visually mark the location of the Yellow Line on the ground in order to reduce friction” with Palestinians.

“Defensive measures,” it said, “are intended to prevent infiltrations and hostile activity, and to protect both the troops and surrounding communities” in Israel.

Those IDF measures include the construction of a berm — a dirt barrier piled high — that the UN says now stretches 23 kilometres, along or behind the yellow line. It towers in the distance over many of the tent camps.

And, increasingly, Israel is building fortified compounds that look like permanent Israeli military bases.

Gaza’s neighbourhoods flattened

Satellite images show one of those military compounds — well inside Gaza — about half way between Israel’s border and the sea. It has permanent guard posts, multiple structures and a paved parking lot — all protected by tanks. Another one, further south in Jabalia, is even larger, and seems more established. Several others are under construction.

Still, Israel isn’t just digging in. It is also tearing down.

Many of Gaza’s neighbourhoods were destroyed during active fighting between Israel and Hamas over two years of war. This came in response to the Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel which left approximately 1,200 Israelis dead.

But as satellite images show, many more homes have been systematically flattened by Israeli forces since last October, after most conflict stopped.

Near the Indonesian hospital in northern Gaza, buildings which were still standing last November are now gone. And in Shejaiya, next to Gaza City, entire swaths of housing that are seen in images from October were blown up or bulldozed by April — on both sides of the yellow line.

Between October 2025 and July 2026, neighbourhoods in Gaza have been completely destroyed because of the advancement of the yellow line. (CBC Visual Investigation Unit)

UN experts have denounced “the systematic detonation of residential buildings,” as “re-engineering the geography of illegally occupied Gaza” by Israel.

Palestinians who have watched their homes destroyed say there’s a plan.

“Israel is trying everything to push the people to leave Gaza,” said Alaa Hajjaj. “To make people’s lives miserable.”

Hajjaj is a teacher, now living with his family in a tent in northern Gaza. The rubble of his house sits well behind the yellow line, a place he’s not sure he will ever be able to reach again.

“But for myself, I am not going to leave Gaza, whatever happens,” Hajjaj said. “This is my home. This is my land. I was born on this land and I have memories here and I have everything in this land.”

‘Gaza is ours,’ Israeli groups claim

Officially, the Israeli government denies it is trying to push out Palestinians or annex Gaza.

But there is strong political pressure to do exactly that, including inside Netanyahu’s party and coalition cabinet.

Extremist settler groups like Nachala have repeatedly marched to the Gaza border, running public relations campaigns with videos underlining their demands.

“The people of Israel will cross this fence, and establish settlements here,” Nachala leader Daniella Weiss said, pointing through the barrier into Gaza.

The yellow line has moved westward since the October ceasefire. Here, a block is visible in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip. (Abdel Kareem Hana/AP)

They have been joined by cabinet members from far-right parties. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir is seen yelling “Gaza is ours,” and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told supporters “there will be no victory” until Jewish settlements are established in Gaza.

Even prominent members of Netanyahu’s own party, Likud, support annexation.

“We are preparing to take hold of the northern part of Gaza,” said Economy Minister Nir Barakat at the border.

Netanyahu himself has skirted the issue, telling one supporter who asked why the IDF should control 70 per cent of Gaza and not all of it, “First 70 per cent. We’ll start with that.”

That may be just talk.

With Israeli elections two months away, and Israeli media predicting Netanyahu is in a tight fight to stay in power, some of that may be political rhetoric aimed to please his own base.

Israel may also be taking a hard line in international negotiations, to pressure Hamas militants to give up their weapons, a move the group has been slow to adopt despite agreeing to it in October’s ceasefire deal.

But for Palestinians moved by yellow markers — and menaced by the guns behind them — there’s a real fear they’re being pushed into the sea.

World.title: With 60 days left until Alberta’s referendum, stay and leave sides plot their course
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Only 60 days remain until Albertans answer 10 questions that could shape the future of the province.

Nine focus on immigration and constitutional reform. But it’s the 10th question — whether Albertans want the province to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on separation — that is increasingly poised to animate town halls and rallies scheduled in the coming days.

And with the clock ticking, both sides have limited opportunities to win over hearts and minds.

That will be a challenge.

Keith Wilson, left, one of the co-leaders of the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide, and Thomas Lukaszuk, right, leader of Forever Canadian, are among leaders organizing their next moves. (Nathan Gross/CBC)

Longtime pollster Janet Brown has been watching the numbers for years. Those numbers have shown, consistently, that support for separatism trails well behind those who back staying in Canada.

“We've seen very little movement in the data over the past eight years,” Brown said. “And very few people remain undecided at this point — in the five per cent to eight per cent range.”

Given that, the referendum campaign is becoming less about persuasion, and more about mobilization, in Brown’s view.

“Voter turnout is critical for both sides,” she said.

There are, of course, many different groups competing for eyeballs on both sides of the debate.

Here’s a look at how four of them say they’ll approach the campaign’s next phase.

Let Alberta Decide

One pro-independence leader says some on the campaign trail have been hesitant to share publicly that they support Alberta independence. He’s not entirely convinced the polls are accurate.

“But from a strategic point of view, we assume they are,” said Keith Wilson with the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide. “So we realize we have an uphill battle.”

The group, which leads all third-party advertisers with more than $415,000 in donations as of Aug. 13, is planning a major rally on Oct. 17 at the Alberta Legislature, two days before the referendum.

Traditional get-out-the-vote operations are planned, including organizing minibuses to drive people to stations.

Keith Wilson with the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide sits behind a series of computer screens in his office, which he calls the “war room.” (Nathan Gross/CBC)

Polling shows support for independence is strongest in rural regions, but weaker in the urban areas, so the group is concentrating efforts in Calgary and Edmonton, as well as smaller cities like Lethbridge and Lloydminster.

It’s also adapting its messaging on social media towards different demographics — for instance, towards young men in their 20s struggling to make rent, or towards senior citizens concerned about their grandchildren's future.

“We're going to be ramping up incrementally as we get closer to the voting day,” Wilson said.

Forever Canadian

Last Friday, volunteers were busy at the Forever Canadian campaign office in Edmonton, stacking lawn signs into wagons before loading them into vehicles.

Organizer Thomas Lukaszuk said the group has teams “literally in every municipality across Alberta,” and plans to visit more towns in Forever Canadian’s “Unity Bus.”

“I think we’re in the second period of a hockey game, but this has been already going on for one year and one month,” Lukaszuk said.

Forever Canadian organizer Thomas Lukaszuk speaks with people at the group’s campaign office in Edmonton on Friday. He said the group’s current priority is fulfilling sign requests and distributing campaign materials. (Nathan Gross/CBC)

Lukaszuk said some large rallies organized by Forever Canadian are planned over the next couple of months, and the group plans to continue distributing its lawn signs across the province.

The group has said it has more than 18,000 Albertans who volunteered to promote unity. As of now, Lukaszuk said he sees the group’s role continuing much as it has been.

“If we pivot into get out the vote, then obviously we have the resources. But at this stage of this campaign, that’s not what we’re focusing on,” he said. “We’re focusing on boosting Canadian pride, and that seems to be a very effective campaign.”

Alberta Prosperity Project/Stay Free Alberta

This group, which led the citizen initiative petition looking to force a vote on Alberta separating from Canada, views October as the culmination of years of work.

Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of Alberta Prosperity Project, said the group plans to maximize advance polls — even if it’s not something it “agrees with” — while holding town halls across Alberta.

“We'll focus on getting people out to vote right now. I think we’ll have a very good chance if we get our people out,” Sylvestre said.

Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, says his group views the coming 60 days as the final push after years of work. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

The group has a rally planned Aug. 29 at the Alberta Legislature, which it refers to as a “gathering for a province in peril.”

In the lead-up to the vote, the group plans to encourage its members to develop a list of close friends and neighbours, ensuring they’re responsible to get them to polls.

Alberta's Voice

Alberta's Voice, run by Decide Campaigns' president Stephen Carter, currently has the most contributions listed for a pro-Confederation campaign, with more than $87,000.

Carter said Alberta’s Voice would like to do an “air war” advertising campaign, buying radio spots in Calgary, Edmonton and rural Alberta.

“But raising funds has been our primary challenge, and we need to make sure that we’re able to compete with the separatists,” Carter said. “The leading separatist group has raised four times as much money as we have.”

The group is also focused on undecided voters and is aiming for a 75-25 split on referendum day in favour of staying in Canada.

“The number one thing to do is to really dig into the undecided voters,” Carter said.

“There’s not many of them, but those that are there are going to make the difference between whether or not we have to face this again in the future, or if we can kill this dead right off the top.”

Alberta’s Voice is behind the “no to the nine” signs. The group is emphasizing the importance of voter turnout, believing low turnout could favour the remain side. (Jennifer Keiller/CBC)

The group plans to establish a campaign college in early September to train volunteers on voter mobilization. It also has designs on a “captain system,” which would involve people emailing and calling others to get to the polls on election day.

“We're hoping to sign up 100,000 people through that mechanism,” Carter said. “And that will enable us to really change, I think, the overall turnout.

“The people who we're targeting aren't necessarily the hyper-engaged, but they're the ones who are adjacent to the hyper-engaged.”

While the referendum is 60 days away, Elections Alberta is also allowing residents to vote by mail — and that deadline comes sooner. Special ballot packages must be received before 5 p.m. on Oct. 16.

World.title: Why invasive plants are still sold in garden centres across Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian cities are trying to stop invasive plants from being sold in local garden centres, as advocates push Ottawa to create a national approach to regulating the horticultural trade.

With invasive plants threatening biodiversity across the country, municipalities are increasingly trying to fill gaps in a regulatory system that varies by jurisdiction. Canada, meanwhile, has set a target of reducing the rate of introduction and establishment of known invasive species by at least 50 per cent by 2030.

The Canadian Coalition for Invasive Plant Regulation (CCIPR) wants the federal government to establish a regulatory body for the horticultural industry and create a national database identifying invasive plants and their risks in different regions.

"Even if we don't prohibit them, we need to let the public know when there is potential harm," said CCIPR co-founder Cathy Kavassalis. "We do this on other products, and we should do it on plants too. It's just common sense."

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency regulates some invasive plants , while provinces and territories have their own invasive species or weed-control legislation.

CBC News reached out to the Canadian Food Inspection Agency for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

Goutweed, an invasive plant, in a garden in Clyde River, P.E.I. (Sara Fraser/CBC)

In July, Nanaimo council passed a motion to pursue a bylaw amendment restricting the sale of plants on a list maintained by the Invasive Species Council of B.C. A week later, Surrey moved to ban sales by businesses including nurseries, large retail chains and florists.

In May, London, Ont.'s, environmental committee recommended requiring retailers that sell invasive plants and animals to provide information to customers at the point of sale.

Kavassalis said a problem that could be addressed at higher levels of government is being pushed down to municipalities.

"These are all patchwork solutions that, in some ways, just waste a lot of resources," she said.

Kirsty MacDonald, Nanaimo's parks manager, said invasive plants are already affecting the local landscape, with some posing potential risks to human health.

Most local plant suppliers were aware of the problem, she said, though invasive species can still appear in plant mixes or popular varieties such as English ivy.

"Banning the sale of new introductions [of invasive plants] in backyards, especially, is one method," she said. "It's a many-pronged approach that we need to be looking at to make some headway."

"All levels of government really need to be part of the solution," she said.

A white trillium is surrounded by periwinkle, an invasive plant sold in some stores, in Inglis Falls Conservation Area in Ontario. (Photo by Andy Fyon, supplied by CCIPR)

What advocates want Ottawa to do

Kavassalis said meeting the federal government's 2030 target will require addressing the horticultural trade.

A 2021 study by University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers identified the sale of ornamental non-native plants as a "primary pathway" for introducing invasive plants in the United States. A 2023 study found plant nurseries could contribute about 80 per cent of invasive plant introductions there.

Kavassalis said the same problem exists in Canada.

"Our gardens are actually the source of a lot of harm being done to our environment and economy," she said.

The CCIPR says a national database could give provinces, territories, retailers and gardeners a shared source of information about which plants pose risks in different regions. Kavassalis also wants invasive plants removed from shelves or clearly labelled.

What would new rules mean for nurseries?

Jim Hole, a horticulture and agriculture expert who previously owned Hole Greenhouses and Gardens in St. Albert, Alta., said most garden centres would support efforts to prevent the spread of invasive plants.

When purple loosestrife was identified as invasive to wetlands, he said his greenhouse stopped selling it.

LISTEN | Invasive plants for sale in London, Ont.: London Morning 7:14 Should invasive plants come with warning labels? A group of Londoners are calling on city council to require garden centres to warn customers about buying invasive plants and pets. Brendon Samuels, a member of the city's environmental stewardship and action community advisory committee, joined London Morning with more details about the pitch.

With thousands of plants available, Hole said removing a species is unlikely to threaten a business.

"It's not like you think, 'Oh well, there goes my business. That was a plant that I made all the money off of,'" he said.

He said stronger research, regulation and public education could also help greenhouse owners and farmers who spend time and money controlling unwanted plants.

"The payback is huge if you can keep even one more invasive species out," he said.

Why gardeners still matter

Native plant advocate and author Lorraine Johnson said consumers often don't know which plants are invasive, while nurseries have significant influence over what people put in their gardens.

She said the horticultural industry is "deeply implicated" in biodiversity loss.

"Their main bread and butter is selling non-native plants, introduced plants that have not co-evolved with those insects that we want to support, [or] with the pollinators," she said.

Native plant gardens are beneficial for pollinators, like bees, that play a key role in ecosystems, said Lorraine Johnson, a native plant advocate and author. (Daniel Thomas/CBC/Radio-Canada)

Kavassalis said regulating garden centres can also help gardeners get past "plant blindness," where every green thing can seem equal.

"We need to help the public … treat the plants in their gardens not simply as garden decor, sort of outdoor living space, but as something that's connected to the greater living world."

World.title: 'I was meant to be there': Off-duty Mountie helps rescue baby, family trapped in house fire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Four people — including two teens and a baby — are survivors of a fast-moving house fire thanks to an off-duty RCMP officer who rushed to their aid and helped a desperate man pull his family out of a basement window.

Const. Anton Lorde was on his way home late in the afternoon from his shift on July 18 when he spotted a plume of dark smoke billowing into the sky. It led him to Mount Pleasant Street in the Whitney Pier neighbourhood of Sydney, N.S.

Lorde arrived to find a house being ravaged by fire, with flames shooting out the front, sides and roof. He assumed no one was home because a number of people were milling about. So he immediately started clearing the narrow street for the arrival of fire trucks.

But when he stopped a neighbour to ask about the homeowner, he was told a lot of people lived there, including kids.

Const. Anton Lorde points to himself in a video taken before he helped rescue four young people trapped in a burning house on July 18 in Sydney, N.S. (Dave Laughlin/CBC)

" I’ll never forget that — it almost seemed like everything froze,” the 10-year veteran of the RCMP said in a recent interview.

The neighbour pointed Lorde to a backyard where he hopped a fence and began banging on windows of the burning building, going from one to the next in case someone was inside.

Suddenly, hands parted the blinds, and the eyes of a shocked boy looked back at him.

“Probably frightened him with some of the things I was saying for him to get out. Then I lost sight of him because he closed the blinds,” Lorde said.

“At that point, my mind is going a mile a minute.”

He continued to pound on the window , yelling for them to get out and calling for someone to pass him something to smash the glass , when the father of the children appeared.

Peter Magliaro, his wife Joleen and three children lived in the home at 250 Mount Pleasant St. (Samuel Murrant/CBC)

In an interview at his burned-out property, Peter Magliaro said he was nearly home when he got a call from his niece that his house was on fire.

As he ran between buildings in "unbearable heat," flames burned his cheek, he said.

"You're not thinking, all that was on my mind was the kids."

He started "hollering" to them, knowing they were at home and that his 13-year-old son was likely sleeping because he plays video games at night.

Then Magliaro started kicking in a basement bedroom window before Lorde ripped away the thick blinds to bust out the glass shards.

Magliaro grabbed the four-month-old baby girl from her mother, who is Magliaro's stepdaughter, and passed her to Lorde. He had no idea Lorde — who wasn't in uniform — was a police officer.

Police and the fire marshal's office are conducting investigations into the fire. (Kyle Moore/CBC)

Magliaro's brother-in-law, who lives on the same street, helped him haul the rest of the children out the window: his teenaged son, and his stepdaughters, who are 15 and 22.

Some details of the rescue are a blur to Lorde, who hails from Uniacke Square in Halifax. But it was not a solo effort.

“There were a number of us that saved lives. I think the older gentleman bringing it to my attention at the time, and then my natural instincts and training kicked in at that point, and then the father or stepfather coming to assist in a time of urgency,” said Lorde.

Magliaro agreed it was three men pulling together, and praised the Mountie.

"That's big, not too many people would do that with the amount of people that were here that day," said Magliaro. "I mean this guy's right there on my back with me."

Lorde said someone hugged him before he left the scene. Another person shook his hand and called him a hero, but he downplayed the suggestion.

“I was meant to be there,” he said.

RCMP Nova Scotia acknowledged on social media Const. Anton Lorde's 'bravery and his willingness to help those in need during a critical moment.' (RCMP Nova Scotia/Facebook)

The municipality said its fire crews were called at 5:30 p.m. and were on scene within six minutes. Fire crews were able to save the family's cat and a rabbit, Magliaro said.

The fire marshal’s office declined to comment, citing an ongoing investigation, and noted Cape Breton Regional Police are also investigating.

In a Facebook post, Magliaro contends the fire was intentionally set and is offering a reward for information leading to the arrest of “the person or people responsible for setting my house on fire while my children were inside.”

Magliaro said his brother-in-law told him "they heard a bang and then the next thing you know the whole front of the house was engulfed in flames."

With both doors to the home ablaze, "somebody had to have set the fire, and it wasn't from the inside," Magliaro said.

Peter Magliaro has offered a reward for information on what he believes is an intentionally set fire and will forward tips to Cape Breton Regional Police. (Peter Magliaro/Facebook)

CBC News asked Cape Breton Regional Police about the allegations in Magliaro's Facebook post.

"We cannot speculate on the cause and/or whether the fire was intentionally set; answering those questions is part of the investigation," police spokesperson Desiree Magnus said in an emailed statement.

Magliaro said he's been told it could take six to eight weeks to learn the results of the fire investigation.

Magliaro and his family are now living in a friend's apartment. He said the house was uninsured but he intends to draw from savings to start rebuilding in the spot where he's lived for 35 years.

World.title: Proposed changes to endangered species law would 'stab it to death,' says scientist
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Five former chairs of a panel that advises the federal government on endangered wildlife have published an open letter highlighting concerns over proposed changes to the Species At Risk Act, which they say could lead to the "wilful extinction" of endangered species in Canada.

More than 600 species are listed under the legislation. Changes the government is considering would render the act — and the protection it provides — "meaningless," according to a press release written by the scientists last week.

The scientists, former chairs of the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC), sent the letter to the federal government last month. COSEWIC is an independent advisory panel that assesses species at risk of extinction and makes recommendations to list them under endangered species law.

The scientists opted to make the letter public so that Canadians could avoid being "complicit in the wilful extinction of Canadian Wildlife Species," according to the press release.

The letter comes as the Carney government considers sweeping changes to environmental regulations, including the Species At Risk Act, it says would allow for quicker approval and construction of major projects.

The future of 'jeopardy tests'

In May, two federal discussion papers proposed the approval of major projects before review and exempting certain projects from the "jeopardy test" required under the law, if they're deemed to be in the national interest.

"This is a sledgehammer to the law. It's not necessary," said David Green, a biologist and professor emeritus at McGill University who is one of the former COSEWIC chairs behind the letter.

Jeopardy tests prohibit Ottawa from authorizing projects that would harm species listed under the act and their critical habitats if they would jeopardize their survival. These jeopardy tests are essential to protecting endangered species, according to Green.

"[Jeopardy tests] are the final hurdle. It's the last-ditch protection for things that really need to be protected."

The proposed changes would also give Carney and his cabinet the ability to establish "federal economic zones" where they could then pre-approve industrial development. Cabinet would also gain the power to pre-approve pipelines before a route is established and exempt them from federal impact assessments.

Bill C-5 currently allows projects deemed in the national interest to have their approval process, including environmental assessments, fast-tracked.

The letter mentions a new West Coast oil pipeline, which is currently being considered as a project of national interest, specifically. The proposed pipeline would carry approximately one million barrels of crude oil a day along roughly 1,250 kilometres using a corridor similar to the existing Trans Mountain pipeline, according to the Alberta government.

This would be detrimental to multiple species listed under the act, including the southern resident killer whale — also known as Orcas — and the Chinook salmon, the whale's main food source, according to the scientists.

Both species and their critical habitats exist in the Salish Sea, a network of coastal waterways in southern B.C., where the proposed West Coast pipeline would end.

A southern resident killer whale swims past a school of salmon near the Fraser River, B.C. Chinook salmon are a main food source of the southern resident. (Keith Holmes/The Canadian Press/Hakai Institute)

"If deemed in the national interest, the currently conceived West Coast pipeline could decimate the entire population of the imperilled killer whales through time both directly via increased tanker traffic noise and indirectly via significant destruction of habitat needed for the whales' main prey," the scientists wrote.

"Are Canadians willing to bet this unique population of killer whales against another oil pipeline?"

There are 75 southern resident killer whales in the world.

An 'extraordinary' precedent

Green said he's shocked the Liberal government is proposing these changes.

"It surprises me because the Species At Risk Act was such an important thing to do for a Liberal government 25 years ago.… And now we have a Liberal government that wants to, you know, stab it to death."

Kathryn Harrison, a UBC professor who specializes in climate and energy politics, believes that through Bill C-5 and other changes under consideration, the government is setting an "extraordinary" precedent.

"It's a pretty extraordinary thing to pass new legislation that not only allows the government to waive application of those laws, but gives the government a certain amount of authority to add new laws," she said.

"Rather than going through Parliament and amending those laws, they're passing a new law saying, 'we're not worried about that anymore.'"



The scientists hadn't received a government response to their letter at the time of this article's publication.

The Privy Council Office said the government is "committed to the conservation and recovery of species at risk and to meeting obligations under the Species at Risk Act," in an emailed statement to CBC News.

The federal government has justified the potential changes by arguing Canada needs to fast-track projects that strengthen the economy and diversify exports away from the U.S., amid the ongoing trade war between the two countries.

The Privy Council Office didn't confirm whether they've received the open letter, but said there's been no decision regarding changes to the Species At Risk Act. The email also said the government will release a report highlighting feedback from all Canadians before summer ends.

Following criticism from First Nations and environmental groups, the government extended the public engagement period, which ended last month.

Formal legislation is expected after Parliament resumes in September. Green is cautioning the government to reconsider.

"If you eliminate species from Canada, they're not coming back," he said.

World.title: Who is Mohammad Ghamira and why has his death, alleged abuse ignited outcry in Syria?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Syrians took to the streets this week to call for justice over the death of Mohammad Ghamira, a Syrian man who died in hospital after alleged abuse by security forces while in detention — less than two years after the new government vowed to break away from the systemic, arbitrary detentions and abuse that was common under the ousted regime.

Ghamira's family said they told police that the 29-year-old father of two suffered from hemophilia, a rare genetic disorder that impairs the body's ability to make blood clots, which can lead to prolonged bleeding.

He was held in detention for three days before being released on Aug. 9 and taken immediately to hospital. He died a week later.

For Syria’s new government, Ghamira’s death has become somewhat of a litmus test of whether its promises of accountability will translate into action after the fall of the Assad's iron-fisted dynasty, which ruled the country for more than 50 years.

Ghamira's death sparked a series of peaceful sit-ins and protests in the country this week, but rights groups say his case is only one of many reports of alleged mistreatment at detention centres that have come out since the new government took power.

"The death of Mohammad Ghamira raises exactly the concerns we have been documenting since the transition began: detention practices that are not yet governed by a unified, judicially supervised system," Fadel Abdulghany, executive director of Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR), told CBC News.

"Syria’s transition will be judged on whether accountability for cases like this becomes systemic, not selective."

Family warned police of dire medical condition

Ghamira was a former volunteer with the White Helmets, also known as the Syria Civil Defence, which was formed in 2013 and operated during the war in opposition-held areas. The group's role shifted from an independent rescue group to part of the country's formal state emergency services after the collapse of the former regime in 2024.

The Latakia Internal Security Command said Ghamira was detained regarding an allegation "that he stole a sum of money." It did not provide any further details.

Members of the White Helmets carry the body of Ghamira, a former White Helmets volunteer who died shortly after his release from jail, before his burial in the village of al-Haffa, Latakia province, Syria, on Monday. (The Associated Press)

While in custody, his family was unable to visit or contact him, and was told only that he was “under investigation," according to the SNHR.

His uncle, Issam Ghamira, told state news agency SANA the family had informed the police chief in al-Haffah that his nephew had hemophilia and warned against hitting him. Despite that, he said, his nephew was hit while in custody.

Ghamira died at the Latakia University Hospital on Sunday after being released from jail.

Syria's Minister of Emergency and Disaster Management Raed al-Saleh mourned the death of his "brother, friend and young colleague."

Al-Saleh, who was previously head of the White Helmets, said on X that Ghamira had died of "complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal hemorrhaging" that "resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained at the al-Haffah police station."

"I affirm to his family and all Syrians that the new Syria is a state of law and justice…. The Syrians have sacrificed throughout 14 years to reach a Syria that upholds their dignity and preserves their humanity, and there will be no impunity in the new Syria," Al-Saleh said.

Police interrogator to be prosecuted

Ghamira was buried Monday in his hometown of al-Haffah in Syria's coastal Latakia province.

Syria's Interior Ministry announced on Sunday an investigation into Ghamira's death. It said seven Interior Ministry personnel were detained for questioning.

On Thursday, Maj. Gen. Ahmed Latouf, head of the committee formed to investigate Ghamira's death, said that medical experts found that he had died of complications from a cerebral hemorrhage.

Latouf said that investigators found that a police interrogator had slapped Ghamira in the neck during interrogation, despite the man having told police personnel about his medical condition.

The interrogator was referred to the public prosecution division and disciplinary investigations into other police personnel are ongoing, he said.

Mourners carry the coffin at Ghamira's funeral on Monday in al-Haffa. (The Associated Press)

The Syria Campaign, a rights group founded in 2014, condemned the committee's findings, saying that while they acknowledge the abuse, they ultimately exonerate government officials.

"The committee's conclusion is not surprising, but it is frightening," it said in a statement on Thursday.

"The issue has never been a single torturer, but rather a system and a mentality that considers violence in detention centres acceptable, and then protects its perpetrators with a culture of impunity."

SNHR's Abdulghany said anyone detained must be informed of the reasons for arrest, brought promptly before an independent judge and able to challenge the lawfulness of detention, in accordance with Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

Abdulghany questioned whether the internal investigation would be enough to provide accountability.

"What matters now is whether the case moves to an independent criminal investigation and prosecution, not an internal disciplinary process alone, and whether the outcome — and the forensic evidence behind it — is made available to the family and the public," Abdulghany said.

Earlier, Syrian Interior Ministry spokesperson Noureddine al-Baba acknowledged on Monday that there were "shortcomings and deficiencies" in some of the country's police departments, adding that he hopes the incident will "serve as a catalyst for positive change" in its operations.

Accountability 'not enough,' families say

Syrians whose loved ones disappeared or died in detention centres during Assad's rule say they were disturbed to hear of ongoing abuse.

"What happened to [Ghamira] reopens the wounds of torture and death in detention for thousands of Syrian families — practices that Syrians have struggled for years to end, and whose recurrence today cannot be tolerated," Families for Freedom, a group representing relatives of detainees, said in a statement written in Arabic on Monday.

WATCH | Documented evidence of torture under former Assad regime: Leaked files expose torture, killing of detainees in Syria | Duration 2:11 Leaked files from Syria’s former regime under dictator Bashar al-Assad reveal new details about the torture and killings of more than 10,000 detainees during the country’s 13-year civil war. The 134,000 Syrian security and intelligence records were obtained by German public broadcaster NDR and shared with the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and its global network of media partners, including CBC News.

The group said it is calling for an "independent and transparent" investigation, along with a publication of the investigation's findings and a formal apology to Ghamira's family.

The organization added that prosecuting abuses after they occur is "not enough," calling instead for systemic reforms to prevent mistreatment, strengthen oversight of detention facilities and ensure such abuses are not repeated.

"A new Syria cannot be built with the old tools of oppression."

Abuses persist in detention centres, rights groups say

When insurgents unseated Assad in December 2024 after a nearly 14-year conflict, they opened the country's notorious prisons. During Assad's rule, thousands of prisoners were killed in mass executions or died from injuries and disease. Detainees were subjected to torture, beatings and rape, according to rights groups that have documented the abuse.

When Syria's transitional government took over, it vowed to uphold the "rule of law" and ensure fair trials and proper judicial oversight during arrests.

Syrians carry the pictures of their relatives, who were killed following the Syrian revolution in March 2011, as they celebrate in front of the Palace of Justice in Damascus on Aug. 11. A Syrian court sentenced former ruler Bashar al-Assad to death after a trial in absentia, convicting him of atrocities committed during the country's nearly 14-year conflict. (Bakr AlKasem/AFP/Getty Images)

Officials with the government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa have promised accountability in Ghamira's case, but rights groups say it is not an isolated incident and that abuses persist in detention centres.

In a new report published last week , Syrians for Truth and Justice, a human rights organization that tracks abuses, said "severe beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, threats, deprivation of basic necessities, and deaths in custody continue to be common practices at the hands of multiple security and military actors."

The group concluded that the incidents were too widespread to treat as isolated incidents but there was not evidence of a "single centralized system equivalent in structure and direction to the torture apparatus entrenched by the Assad regime."

"It is somehow widespread, but it's not structured," Bassam Alahmad, the group's executive director, told The Associated Press on Monday. "For us, there is no evidence that these orders came from the commanders to torture people, but still [the authorities] have a responsibility to stop this behaviour."

In an earlier report released in March, the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic said it had documented "torture and ill-treatment" in 18 official detention facilities and 12 "makeshift facilities" in different areas of Syria between January and October 2025.

World.title: Soccer fans launch global petition urging FIFA boss Infantino to resign over World Cup 'betrayal'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A collection of soccer fan groups from around the world launched a petition Thursday calling for Gianni Infantino to resign as FIFA president after he tried to sell future World Cup profits to private investors.

The petition with the hashtag InfantinOut also calls for "FIFA to be rebuilt so that the current debacle can never happen again."

"The shameful attempt by one individual — the FIFA President himself — to sell off the World Cup to private investors exposed a betrayal football will never forget," the petition said about Infantino's plan for a commercial spinoff, which he dropped amid a furious backlash.

The fan groups include Football Supporters Europe, Football Supporters Africa and, in North America, the Independent Supporters Council, plus about 40 national fan groups worldwide.

WATCH | Can Infantino's FIFA presidency survive after sell-off plan?: Can FIFA's president survive this? | About That | Duration 2:10 Avneet Dhillon breaks down the open letter to FIFA from several soccer federations accusing President Gianni Infantino of deception over his proposal to sell a portion of the World Cup to private investors. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Infantino has resisted calls to leave office despite European soccer body UEFA saying it has no confidence in him. He has also been criticized by the leadership of North America's CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation.

"Gianni Infantino has demonstrated a profound failure of leadership, incompatible with democratic governance," the fan petition states. "The concentration of power around the FIFA Presidency, combined with opaque decision-making, personality cult clientelism, and zero accountability has destroyed any remaining trust in the world governing body."

"For the credibility of FIFA — and for the future of the game — he must resign," the petition adds.

It also cites Infantino's past support for projects that angered fans, including the failed European Super League project and pushing to hold World Cups every two years.

World.title: Can generation Z save the West?: Etienne A. Beauregard deconstructs Anti-Civilization
World.content:
Article content

Etienne Alexandre Beauregard joins the National Post’s Terry Newman to discuss his new book, “Anti-Civilization: The Collapse of Society and the Case for the Common Good.” Beauregarde argues the West is experiencing a profound crisis due to the excessive emphasis placed on individualism over common good and the absence of shared norms, typically transmitted through generations. Beauregarde argues that the isolation this societal change has created has deeply affected generation Z.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.
