World.title: Mikee Romero retires from AFP Reserve Force amid medals controversy
World.content:
The former congressman also relinquishes his post as wing commander of the Tactical Operations Wing Reserve Northern Luzon 'effective immediately'

MANILA, Philippines – Businessman and former 1-Pacman congressman Michael “Mikee” Romero has retired from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Reserve Force, amid questions raised over his military awards.

“With gratitude and respect, I hereby formally relinquish all my duties and responsibilities as Wing Commander of the Tactical Operations Wing Reserve Northern Luzon and retire from the Reserve Force of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), effective immediately,” Romero said in a letter addressed to AFP chief General Antonio Nafarrete dated August 19.

Romero, who held the rank of brigadier general in the Philippine Air Force (PAF) Reserve, made the move days after his photo with Nafarrete made the rounds on social media. The photo showed the former congressman in uniform with seemingly more medals than the AFP chief himself, raising questions about how Romero, a reserve officer, got so many medals in the first place.

Among the medals allegedly spotted on Romero was the Gold Cross Medal, which is the fourth highest military award given to personnel for acts of gallantry. Romero denied this and said his Gawad sa Kapayapaan medal — for helping the AFP acquire three new C-130 aircraft when he was still a congressman — was mistaken for the Gold Cross Medal.

An example of a Gold Cross Medal recipient is Scout Ranger Captain Gromel Auman, who was killed in action during a firefight with Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters (BIFF) on March 8, 2015.

On Wednesday, August 19, the AFP said in a statement that it was “reviewing its policies and procedures on the recruitment, promotion, and conferment of awards to personnel of the Reserve Force.”

The AFP said it “remains committed to upholding the integrity, meritocracy, and credibility of its processes. Any verified irregularities shall be addressed in accordance with existing rules and regulations.”

“The AFP recognizes the valuable contributions of its reservists and will continue to ensure that the standards governing the Reserve Force are properly observed,” it added.

The AFP also cited an ongoing PAF investigation into the matter.

The PAF said the investigation will address concerns regarding the promotions and decorations to reserve personnel. It said this will include a review “of the affected personnel records, orders, and promotion boards.”

“Any verified irregularities or policy violations resulting from this investigation will be dealt with decisively under existing rules and regulations to preserve the credibility and standards of the Air Force Reserve Service,” the PAF said.

Among those who backed the review was Senate Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, a Philippine Military Academy graduate who had served in the Philippine Constabulary and the Philippine National Police.

“Behind every ribbon pinned on a soldier’s uniform represents a medal. Every medal has a unique story about heroism, valor, courage and bravery, or an outstanding feat even outside the combat zone,” Lacson said in a social media post on Wednesday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Reintroduced Tiger Shows Early Signs of Successful Adaptation in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ALMATY – Umit, the female Amur tiger released into the wild in Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on July 31, has successfully begun hunting independently, killing a wolf and a wild boar during her first 10 days in her new natural habitat, according to specialists monitoring her adaptation.

The tiger is being tracked daily using a GPS collar, which allows specialists to monitor her movements and identify areas where she has spent time. Field teams then inspect these locations to assess her behavior and adaptation to life in the wild, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.

The successful hunts are an important early indication that Umit is adapting to her new environment and beginning to live independently under natural conditions. Specialists continue to monitor her movements daily and conduct field inspections of areas identified through GPS tracking.

The results of the first 10 days suggest that Umit’s adaptation to independent life in Kazakhstan’s wild is progressing successfully.

World.title: Muay Thai Legends Bring Sports Diplomacy to Kazakhstan, Says Ambassador
World.content:
ASTANA — Muay Thai is deepening cultural ties between Thailand and Kazakhstan by creating connections beyond language and politics, Ambassador of Thailand to Kazakhstan Piyapin Niyomrerks told The Astana Times. Her comments came as three prominent fighters opened a two-day Muay Thai master class in Astana on Aug. 20.

“Beyond sports and competition, soft power like our cuisine, our sport and our Muay Thai has always been a pillar of our bilateral relations with Kazakhstan and Central Asia. Even though we have a language barrier – I don’t speak Kazakh, I don’t speak Russian – everyone on the street knows the words Tom Yum, Muay Thai and Phuket. This is how soft power goes beyond the language barrier, goes beyond politics, and creates bonds of friendship through the love of sports,” said Niyomrerks.

Muay Thai champions arrive in Astana

The Muay Thai master class at the Kazakh National University of Sports (KNUS) brings together athletes, coaches, young fighters and enthusiasts for training with internationally renowned Thai fighter Buakaw Banchamek.

Buakaw, a two-time K-1 World MAX champion, is one of the best-known figures in international Muay Thai. His career also includes four World Muaythai Council titles, championships in two divisions at Omnoi Stadium and the 2016 Kunlun Fight Muay Thai Middleweight World Championship.

He was joined by Marie Ruumet, known as the “Snow Leopard,” the current Rajadamnern Stadium female flyweight champion, and Nuenglanlek Jitmuangnon, nicknamed “Million Horsepower,” a former Rajadamnern Stadium interim welterweight and Omnoi Stadium champion.

Niyomrerks said the idea for the event emerged several months ago after she and embassy representatives attended a youth championship organized by the Kazakhstan Muay Thai Federation and saw more than 500 athletes competing in under-16 and under-18 categories.

“That was the first time I witnessed 500 of the young ones wearing Muay Thai kits. They were so determined and were in such a good spirit. We were so proud to see all these 500 children wearing Muay Thai kits and with Muay Thai flags on their sleeves,” she said.

The embassy initially planned to invite Thai instructors to conduct a master class and teach Wai Kru, the traditional pre-fight ritual performed by Muay Thai fighters. Niyomrerks said the Sports Authority of Thailand recognized Kazakhstan’s strong Muay Thai community and proposed bringing prominent professional fighters.

“After we opened the registration, I think we had over 600 who registered. They even had to close the registration; otherwise, it would go to 800,” she said, highlighting that public interest exceeded initial expectations.

The two-day program features practical training sessions with the visiting fighters, Wai Kru demonstrations, Muay Boran performances showcasing the traditional Thai martial art that preceded modern Muay Thai, and a presentation on Muay Thai’s history. Participants also receive information on training opportunities in Thailand.

Sport expands bilateral exchanges

The Royal Thai Embassy in Astana organized the master class with Thailand’s Ministry of Tourism and Sports, National Sports Development Fund and Boxing Sports Commission, with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Tourism and Sports and Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Deputy Foreign Minister Alibek Kuantyrov told The Astana Times that sports and cultural exchanges have become another area of cooperation alongside political and economic relations between Kazakhstan and Thailand.

“This experience shows that relations between Kazakhstan and the Kingdom of Thailand are developing not only in the economic and political spheres, but also in sport. For the first time, stars of this level in world Muay Thai are coming to Astana, and this gives an opportunity for our young athletes to communicate with them personally, get motivation and learn from their experience,” he said.

Kuantyrov highlighted that such exchanges are particularly valuable for young athletes, schoolchildren and those considering taking up Muay Thai, giving them direct access to experienced fighters and information about the sport’s traditions and training opportunities.

“The most important thing is cultural exchange, when our young athletes, schoolchildren and children who are interested, who are actively training or who are only planning to enter this martial art, have an opportunity to communicate with world stars, gain motivation and receive advice,” said Kuantyrov.

World.title: Kazakhstan Begins Construction of Robotics Complex as It Expands Humanoid AI Ambitions
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has begun construction of its first Robotics & AI complex on Aug. 18. According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, the complex will support research, software and artificial intelligence development, testing and localized production of robotic systems as the country seeks to build domestic capabilities in humanoid robotics.

The project was announced at the QAZBOT ROBOTICS FORUM 2026, held at the alem.ai International Artificial Intelligence Center in Astana on Aug. 19. The facility is intended to form the company’s production and research infrastructure, bringing together research and development, software and AI model development, testing, adaptation and localized production of robotic systems.

Kazakh Deputy Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov said the forum reflected efforts to translate international technology cooperation into concrete projects.

“For us, it is important that cooperation with leading technology companies translates into concrete projects, including the localization of solutions, training of engineering personnel and the introduction of robotics in key sectors of the economy,” Baitursynov said.

From importing robots to building local capabilities

According to QAZBOT Technologies CEO Vladislav Safarov, the company aims to develop a full technological cycle in Kazakhstan, from research and development and software to AI models, localized production and the training of engineers.

“For us, it is essential that the development of robotics in Kazakhstan is not limited to importing ready-made solutions,” Safarov said. “Our task is to create Kazakhstan’s own industrial and engineering base in Robotics & AI and, together with international partners, bring these technologies to practical application.”

The new complex is expected to provide infrastructure for this process, while cooperation with international companies is intended to support technology localization and adaptation to domestic market needs.

During the demonstration program, AgiBot humanoid robots showcased their ability to interact with people, coordinate movements and perform complex tasks, including traditional dance and martial arts movements.

The forum also included business-to-business meetings between QAZBOT Technologies, AgiBot and Kazakh companies, focusing on industry-specific challenges and opportunities to launch pilot projects. Several strategic agreements with Kazakh and international partners were signed during the event in technology, education and international cooperation.

The launch of construction and the agreements reached at the forum mark an effort to move Kazakhstan’s robotics agenda from demonstrations and technology imports toward pilot projects, localized production and the development of an engineering base capable of supporting wider adoption of robotics and AI solutions across the economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Revised Foreign Policy Concept Preserves Balanced Course
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s updated Foreign Policy Concept for 2020–2030 preserves the country’s balanced and pragmatic foreign policy while adapting it to a new constitutional framework, shifting geopolitical realities and a stronger emphasis on protecting the interests of Kazakh citizens and businesses abroad, analysts say. The amendments, signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and effective from Aug. 14, do not introduce a new foreign policy doctrine. Instead, experts describe them as an effort to update the existing framework to reflect both Kazakhstan’s evolving state institutions and a more complex international environment.

A balanced foreign policy remains, but its implementation is evolving

Despite the institutional changes, the most significant continuity in the revised document may be the preservation of Kazakhstan’s balanced and pragmatic approach to foreign policy.

According to the CCBS analytical agency, supported by the Caspian-Black Sea Studies Foundation, the revision matters less for changing Kazakhstan’s core foreign policy course than for adapting it to an increasingly complex international environment.

“Tokayev himself has repeatedly emphasized in recent months the need for a maximally balanced foreign policy focused primarily on protecting Kazakhstan’s national sovereignty and strategic interests,” the agency wrote.

The revision comes amid broader changes in Kazakhstan’s international engagement, including expanding ties with China and the European Union. According to CCBS, Kazakhstan’s engagement with both partners has become more prominent, illustrating the continued relevance of maintaining relations with multiple centers of political and economic influence.

For Zhanat Momynkulov, a political scientist and senior lecturer at the Gumilyov Eurasian National University, this balanced and pragmatic approach remains an important mechanism for preserving Kazakhstan’s strategic autonomy, Qaz365 reported.

“Astana seeks to maintain the ability to interact simultaneously with different centers of power based on its own national interests. Kazakhstan’s balanced and pragmatic foreign policy in 2026 is no longer simply a diplomatic principle but an instrument for managing geopolitical risks,” he said, arguing that the country’s diplomatic approach has evolved alongside a changing international environment.

A foreign policy concept aligned with the new constitutional system

The revised document also incorporates the terminology of Kazakhstan’s new constitutional model.

References to Parliament have been replaced with the Kurultai, which the updated concept defines as the country’s highest representative body exercising legislative power.

Other changes are more technical but still reflect the broader legal transition. The term “citizen” has been replaced with the more specific “citizen of the Republic of Kazakhstan,” while “Independence” and “Sovereignty” are now capitalized. These amendments may appear editorial, but together they align one of Kazakhstan’s principal strategic foreign policy documents with the terminology and institutional architecture established under the new Constitution.

Taken together, the revisions show that the document is being updated not only in response to changes in the international environment but also to reflect Kazakhstan’s domestic political and legal transformation.

Greater focus on citizens and business abroad

Another important shift is the stronger emphasis on the practical protection of Kazakhstan’s interests beyond its borders.

The updated concept calls for greater efforts to promote and protect the interests of the state, domestic businesses and every citizen of Kazakhstan abroad. The document describes this as an important condition for building a strong, harmonious and socially responsible state integrated into the modern international system.

The revised concept also strengthens provisions on protecting the rights and legitimate interests of Kazakh citizens abroad, including Kazakh children adopted by foreign citizens and living outside the country. This reflects what could be described as a more citizen-centered dimension of foreign policy.

Momynkulov said this approach suggests that foreign policy is increasingly expected to produce practical benefits for the country’s citizens and economy.

From personalized continuity to institutional continuity

One of the amendments concerns the concept of foreign policy continuity. The previous version referred specifically to the continuity of the foreign policy course of the former President Nursultan Nazarbayev. That wording has now been replaced with a broader reference to the “continuity of the foreign policy course at a new stage of the country’s development.”

The concept also removes provisions concerning Nazarbayev’s special role in foreign policy, including his previously stipulated lifelong right, based on his historical mission, to address the people, state bodies and officials with initiatives on major foreign policy issues.

According to Momynkulov, the change represents a broader institutional transformation.

“The main change is the depersonalization of foreign policy continuity. Now, only the ‘continuity of the foreign policy course at a new stage of the country’s development’ is established,” he said.

In practical terms, this means that continuity is increasingly defined through the state and its institutions rather than through a particular political figure.

The amendments therefore appear to reflect not a departure from Kazakhstan’s long-standing foreign policy direction but a change in how that continuity is formally defined and institutionalized.

World.title: After Ending Power Shortages Kazakhstan Can Become Electricity Exporter
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan plans to commission 845 megawatts of new power generation capacity in 2027 as part of a broader effort to meet growing electricity demand and build a reserve in the national power system. The planned projects combine gas-fired generation with renewable energy, reflecting the country’s strategy to expand capacity through multiple sources rather than relying on a single type of generation.

According to the Energy Ministry, the new facilities are expected to allow Kazakhstan to fully cover its electricity needs as early as the first quarter of 2027. By the end of the year, the country expects to generate an electricity surplus of around 1.3 billion kilowatt-hours.

The 2027 expansion follows a larger planned capacity increase in 2026, when Kazakhstan expects to commission around 2.6 gigawatts of new generation. This includes four gas-fired power plants, expansions of two existing power stations and 10 new renewable energy facilities.

Together, the plans suggest that the government is seeking not only to close the gap between electricity supply and demand, but also to create additional capacity that could provide greater flexibility for the power system.

Gas and renewables form the core of new capacity

Several conventional generation projects are scheduled to be completed in 2027. Five gas turbine units at the Zhambyl State District Power Plant are expected to add a combined 210 MW. A combined-cycle gas plant at MAEK is planned to provide 160 MW, while the first stage of the Baskuat Energoprom project will add 34.7 MW through five gas piston units.

Another combined-cycle plant, developed by Kazakhmys Energy, is expected to contribute 70 MW. At the same time, the government plans to continue expanding renewable generation, with projects totaling 570 MW.

These include a 100-MW solar power plant in the Almaty Region and three solar projects in the Kyzylorda Region with a combined capacity of 70 MW. Wind projects include two 100-MW facilities in the Aktobe Region, a 50-MW wind power plant in the Kyzylorda Region, another 50-MW project in the Turkistan Region and two wind facilities in the Abai Region with a combined capacity of 100 MW.

The planned renewable projects account for a substantial part of the capacity expansion, while gas-fired facilities are intended to provide additional dispatchable generation. This mix is particularly important for a power system that needs both new electricity volumes and generation that can respond to changes in demand.

From meeting demand to building a reserve

The expected 1.3 billion kilowatt-hour surplus by the end of 2027 marks an important shift in the government’s projections. The objective is no longer limited to covering immediate electricity consumption but also includes creating a reserve that could strengthen the reliability of the national grid.

However, installed generation capacity and actual electricity output are not identical. The amount of electricity ultimately available to the system will depend on factors including the operating performance of new plants, fuel supply, grid infrastructure and, in the case of wind and solar projects, weather conditions.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Confectionery Producers Expand Export Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh confectionery producer LOTTE Rakhat plans to enter the markets of South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, expanding the international reach of one of the country’s established confectionery brands.

The company operates production facilities in Almaty and Shymkent, with combined annual capacity exceeding 100,000 tons. Its range includes more than 500 products, from chocolate and sweets to biscuits and wafers, reported the Agriculture Ministry on Aug. 18.

Export geography

Exports account for around 22% of LOTTE Rakhat’s sales. Russia remains the main destination, receiving around 65% of export shipments. The company also supplies markets in Afghanistan, Central Asia, China, Germany, Mongolia and the South Caucasus. Deliveries to Latvia began in 2026.

The planned expansion to South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand would further diversify the company’s foreign markets. State financial and insurance instruments for domestic producers are also supporting efforts to enter new markets.

Investment and production

LOTTE Rakhat has invested nearly 19.4 billion tenge (US$42 million) in technological development and capacity expansion in recent years. More than 7.1 billion tenge (US$15.4 million) was directed to the Shymkent facility, including new wafer and corn snack production.

The company produces more than 80 types of chocolate bars and maintains an integrated production chain, including processing cocoa beans and producing cocoa mass, cocoa butter and cocoa powder.

Its production system is certified under ISO and HACCP standards and meets Halal requirements. In June, LOTTE Rakhat won the regional Best Product of Kazakhstan 2026 competition in the best food products category.

New capacity in Kostanai

Another major development in the sector is Bayan Sulu’s launch of the Confectionery Capital complex in the Kostanai Region.

The facility will add 16,600 tons of annual capacity, mainly for biscuits and other confectionery products. Investment has reached 14.6 billion tenge (US$31.6 million), with total investment expected to rise to 20 billion tenge (US$43.3 million) after additional production lines are installed.

The project aims to expand domestic processing and increase production of higher-value food products. Bayan Sulu already supplies products to the CIS, European markets and China.

Wider export potential

Together, the developments show the expansion of Kazakhstan’s confectionery manufacturing base and its focus on international markets.

For LOTTE Rakhat, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand are the next potential export destinations. Bayan Sulu expects additional capacity to support production growth and further exports.

LOTTE Rakhat’s history dates to 1942, when confectionery factories from Moscow and Kharkiv were evacuated to Almaty. The Almaty Confectionery Factory became Rakhat JSC in 1992. In 2013, South Korean confectionery company LOTTE Confectionery acquired a controlling stake.

The sector is thus combining expanded production capacity, product development and wider export geography to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in higher-value food manufacturing.

World.title: What Kazakhstan’s Recent Elections Reveal About Voter Participation
World.content:
ASTANA – Voter turnout in Kazakhstan has fluctuated considerably in recent national elections, with presidential contests drawing higher participation than the two most recent parliamentary votes, as experts point to party mobilization, geography and public trust as key factors.

Turnout is not just how many people cast ballots. It can also offer insight into political engagement and parties’ ability to mobilize supporters, particularly in parliamentary elections centered on party competition.

Recent elections also suggest a difference between presidential and parliamentary contests. According to figures from the Central Election Commission, turnout reached 77.5% in the 2019 presidential election and 69.44% in the 2022 presidential vote, compared with 63.3% in the 2021 parliamentary election and 54.15% in the March 2023 parliamentary vote.

Aigul Sadvokasova, director of the Almaty-based Institute of Philosophy, Political Science, and Religious Studies, said presidential elections tend to generate greater voter participation because the choice is centered more directly on individual candidates. Parliamentary elections, by contrast, depend more heavily on voters’ interest in political parties and their platforms.

Sadvokasova made the comments during an Aug. 13 meeting of the Sailau-2026: The Nature of the Political Campaign expert platform in Almaty, organized by the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan.

Historically, national turnout figures also mask substantial regional differences.

For example, in the 2023 parliamentary election, participation varied sharply between Kazakhstan’s largest cities and several regions. Turnout ranged from 25.82% in Almaty to more than 60% in several regions.

Zhenisbek Tolen, head of the Center for Educational Sciences and Social Development at Kazakhstan’s National Academy of Sciences, said regional electorates should not be viewed as homogeneous. Voters in regional capitals and remote districts, as well as younger and older people and different occupational groups, can have significantly different priorities.

“A region is not a single voter. It is made up of different social groups, and a party’s success depends on how effectively a strong local team can speak to each of them in a language they understand,” Tolen said, addressing the expert meeting.

Sadvokasova said turnout is shaped by a broader set of factors, including where voters live, trust in political institutions, access to information, whether citizens feel they can influence political processes and how competitive they perceive an election to be.

Those factors may take on an important role in a parliamentary election. Under Kazakhstan’s current electoral system, all 145 Kurultai deputies are elected through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency, meaning voters choose a party rather than individual candidates within its list.

In a comment to The Astana Times, Riccardo Pelizzo, dean of Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Public Policy, also emphasized the role of mobilization. Election results, he said, reflect not only voter preferences but also whether parties can persuade their supporters to actually cast ballots.

According to Pelizzo, who discussed voter turnout and electoral participation on The Astana Times’ podcast earlier this year, electoral success depends on the “ability to mobilize voters, to bring voters to the polls and to have high turnout levels.”

The Astana Times has followed the race through weekly reviews, from the parties’ initial policy pitches and regional campaigning to the first televised debate, an education-focused debate, and the final campaign week’s focus on the rule of law.

Experts say the current campaign has unfolded in a more active information environment, with parties stepping up outreach to voters and making greater use of televised debates and digital communications. But visibility during a campaign does not automatically translate into participation. One of the central challenges for political parties is sustaining voters’ interest through election day.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election Attracts 777 Foreign Observers
World.content:
ASTANA – A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election, Central Election Commission (CEC) Secretary Mukhtar Yerman said on Aug. 18.

The figure includes 138 members of parliaments from 41 countries.

International monitoring

According to the CEC, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs submitted 121 observer candidates from 18 countries and five international organizations for accreditation.

The observers include representatives of the CIS Observer Mission, the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Turkic Academy.

National observers include representatives from Belgium, China, France, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Japan, Jordan, Mongolia, the Philippines, Serbia, Slovakia, Thailand, Türkiye, Turkmenistan, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Uzbekistan.

CEC Chairman Nurlan Abdirov said the presence of foreign observers contributes to the campaign’s openness and transparency and demonstrates Kazakhstan’s continued cooperation with foreign states and international organizations in the electoral sphere.

Representatives of the central election bodies of 22 countries are also taking part, including 11 heads of election commissions, he said.

First test of the new system

The election will be the first nationwide vote under Kazakhstan’s new parliamentary model. Citizens will elect 145 members of the Kurultai, a new unicameral Parliament, through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency.

Seven political parties are contesting the election. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to enter the legislature.

The new system replaces the previous bicameral Parliament and removes single-member constituencies from national parliamentary elections. The vote will therefore provide an early indication of how the redesigned system affects party competition, political representation and the composition of the legislature.

The campaign has also placed greater emphasis on party platforms. Nationally televised debates have focused on areas including agriculture, social policy, economic development, environmental protection and the rule of law.

Political observers have described the debates as a test of whether parties can present distinct policy positions and respond to public scrutiny.

What international observers will assess

The presence of international observers adds a separate layer of assessment to the election.

Their work will provide an external view of how the new electoral framework operates in practice. The monitoring will also contribute to broader international understanding of Kazakhstan’s parliamentary and electoral reforms.

The number of observers is therefore significant not only as a measure of international attention, but also as part of the transparency surrounding the first Kurultai election.

The election is scheduled for Aug. 23. Its immediate results will show which parties cross the 5% threshold and how the 145 seats are distributed.

The longer-term test will be how the new Kurultai functions under the redesigned parliamentary system and whether the changes strengthen political representation and institutional accountability.

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: ‘We are not on our knees, we are fighting for justice’: David Babayan’s message from Baku prison
World.content:
David Babayan’s message from a Baku prison

“What kind of trial was it? It was a theatrical performance, with the script written in advance,” David Babayan, the former foreign minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, said in a message from a Baku prison.

Babayan’s family gave the audio recording of his message to an Armenian media outlet. In his message, he discusses the trial of the former NKR’s military and political leadership. Two weeks ago, the Court of Appeal upheld the verdicts handed down by the Baku Military Court. In February 2026, David Babayan received a life sentence. He described the Court of Appeal’s ruling as a “formal stage” that had to be completed before the case could be taken to an international court.

“One interesting development was that one of the defence lawyers here [at the Baku court] said they did not want the case to reach an international court because more than 95% of the charges were fabricated and there was no evidence. That is exactly what happened,” Babayan said.

He also said that he and other prisoners were facing serious health problems. He stressed that despite their difficult situation, they were fighting for justice, freedom and human rights.

“It is one thing to fight and stand up for justice, and another to sit in prison for it. But know this: although we are imprisoned, we are not on our knees,” Babayan concluded.

On 5 February 2026, the Baku Military Court sentenced former president Arayik Harutyunyan, Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, deputy commander Davit Manukyan, parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and foreign minister David Babayan to life imprisonment. The court sentenced former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan to 20 years in prison. Baku brought serious charges against all the defendants, ranging from terrorism to genocide. The two former presidents received shorter sentences because of their age. Under Azerbaijani law, courts cannot sentence people over 65 to life imprisonment. The case of former state minister Ruben Vardanyan was heard separately. On 17 February, a Baku court sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

Falsifications instead of evidence

“Remarkably, instead of evidence, they use substitutes here: lies, falsifications, toasts, various political approaches, slogans and so on.

We pointed out that the legal system and the courts cannot operate like the food or chemical industries, where people use substitutes.

Nothing can replace facts and evidence.

But that is how things work in this court. And that is their general approach to us.

Moreover, these falsifications and lies remain in their archives. At times, we tried to see how they recorded all this in their documents. We found that they had not included our statements at all or, at best, had included heavily shortened or distorted versions. This is nothing other than legal apartheid.”

On the old and new charges against him

“What is happening here is simply unimaginable. For example, they automatically attribute a crime committed by one person to everyone.

They added two life-sentence charges to my case that had never appeared before and had never been mentioned throughout the entire first-instance trial. I noticed this when they gave us a brief summary a week after the trial ended. This is unacceptable.

I asked them to review our statements — both my final statement at the first-instance trial and the main statements we made during this trial — and provide them in video format to Azerbaijan’s human rights ombudsman. But they refused.

They say the trial is open, but refuse to provide all the information even to their own human rights ombudsman.

One interesting phenomenon was that five or six defence lawyers changed during this period. One of them changed at the very beginning of the appeal proceedings. I tried to find out why. They told me it was because of health problems. During the hearing, I said: ‘Contact him by video. I want to ask him about his health personally.’ Of course, they became uncomfortable and did not put us in contact. They said his life was not in danger.

They sentenced me to life imprisonment under an article alleging that I had tried to seize power here [in Azerbaijan] and overthrow the constitutional order.

I asked whether there was any evidence that I had taken part in a struggle for power while I was here. If that were the case, I would have had supporters across your country and cells belonging to some organisation. Of course, I received no answer.

The court accepted 100% of our complaints in favour of the prosecution. At the first-instance trial, 99.4% of them went in favour of the prosecution.

I thanked them for mistakes of such quality and quantity because they are very important for us. They will help justice prevail because we will present all of this to an international court.”

Selected groups of people were brought to the hearings on special buses

“There were no Azerbaijani citizens at the Court of Appeal hearings, whereas the first-instance trial always had around 200-300 people in attendance.

Of course, they selected all of them specifically and brought them in on special buses. We saw this.

According to some reports, they were also paid well. But no one attended this trial.

One reason is that these people saw the abuses that took place there. They saw the weak position of their own side, our independent defence, our persistence and the quality of our self-defence. Naturally, whether they wanted it or not, all this information reached their society. That is why they banned these people from attending.”

David Babayan’s message from a Baku prison

World.title: A Gal-Media TV station building has burned down in Abkhazia
World.content:
In Abkhazia, a building housing the regional TV company Gal-Media has been destroyed by fire. Without their equipment, journalists now plan to film their reports using smartphones.

The TV company, which serves the predominantly ethnic Georgian Gali district, occupied several rooms in a four-storey building. The fire destroyed the editing room, recording room and studio where the main news bulletins were produced. It also destroyed all the studio equipment, the server room and the entire archive.

Security camera footage helped investigators identify the exact point where the fire started. It broke out near the ceiling, where a layer of soundproofing foam had been installed. Specialists believe an old bundle of electrical wiring may have caused the fire. Although the premises underwent renovations in 2016, workers did not replace this old section of wiring.

Gali district administration head Konstantin Pilia said emergency services were investigating the incident and expected to release their findings in the coming days. Specialists are also assessing the extent of the damage and the cost of repairs and replacement equipment. The district and republican authorities have already begun taking steps to restore the TV station’s operations.

Because of the fire, Gal-Media will continue operating on a limited basis. Journalists will temporarily use their surviving personal smartphones and laptops to prepare reports. This will allow them to publish information on social media. However, the station’s regular analogue broadcasts will be suspended for the time being, Gal-Media head Thea Arshba said.

The Gali district administration is already looking for temporary premises for the TV company’s staff while repairs are under way.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Gal-Media TV station premises destroyed by fire in Abkhazia

World.title: From C5 to C6: how Azerbaijan is reshaping balance of power in Central Asia
World.content:
Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

On 16 November 2025, the five Central Asian states accepted Azerbaijan as a full member of the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State. Eight months later, on 31 July, Ilham Aliyev took his place at the table at an informal summit in Cholpon-Ata not as a guest, but as one of six equal participants.

The format is now officially known as “Central Asia and Azerbaijan”. The term “C6” has already entered expert vocabulary and is being used at conferences.

The change expands Central Asia’s political and economic cooperation to the western shore of the Caspian Sea. It also turns Azerbaijan from an external partner into a full participant in a route connecting the region with Turkey and Europe.

How did the format emerge and why has it expanded?

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the idea of a consultative mechanism at the UN in September 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana on 15 March 2018. The format’s advantage was its simplicity: without a treaty, permanent secretariat or supranational bodies, the leaders of the five countries could directly discuss borders, water resources, trade and security.

Azerbaijan did not join the process immediately. Ilham Aliyev attended meetings in Dushanbe in 2023, Astana in 2024 and Tashkent in 2025 as an honorary guest. Since the beginning of 2023, he has visited Central Asian countries 16 times, while the region’s leaders have travelled to Azerbaijan 26 times. In 2025, Azerbaijan’s trade with the five Central Asian states grew by 53% to $1.8 billion. Trade among the Central Asian countries themselves reached $10.7 billion in 2024.

Mirziyoyev described Baku’s accession as an opportunity to create a “single space for cooperation” between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Aliyev, in turn, described the two shores of the Caspian as a “single geopolitical and geoeconomic space”.

The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan said they supported expanding the format because it would create new opportunities for transit, logistics and energy cooperation.

The Middle Corridor and the Caspian’s role in bringing the region together

The geography offers the clearest explanation for Azerbaijan’s participation in the format. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with Europe: goods travel by rail across Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, then across the Caspian Sea to Alat, before continuing through Georgia towards Turkey and the Black Sea. Azerbaijan effectively serves as the western gateway to the route.

According to the Kazakh government, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian route rose by 62% in 2024 to 4.5 million tonnes. Baku says the volume of cargo travelling through the Azerbaijani section of the Middle Corridor has increased by 90% over three years. The authorities plan to raise the capacity of the Port of Alat to 25 million tonnes a year. The World Bank estimates that if countries coordinate border procedures, tariffs, port operations and transport schedules, freight volumes along the corridor could triple by 2030, while delivery times could fall by half.

The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Armenian prime minister’s wife launches campaign against domestic violence
World.content:
Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

The wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Anna Hakobyan, has announced the launch of a campaign against domestic violence. She received death threats shortly after calling for a public discussion of the issue. However, she continues to actively promote her initiative.

“The first stage will involve drafting comprehensive and effective legislation and discussing it in the National Assembly,” she said.

According to Anna Hakobyan, the Criminal Code should define domestic violence separately as “a distinct and independent crime”. She plans to invite female MPs from the parliament’s two opposition factions to join her initiative. If they do, she believes there is a chance that “parliament will unanimously approve the bill”.

Anna Hakobyan calls for a “family model with no place for violence”

The prime minister’s wife posted a video message on social media in which she said she intended to continue fighting domestic violence. According to Hakobyan, Armenia’s traditional family model, which hides various forms of violence, should give way to a model of a “family with no place for violence, based on mutual love and respect”. She proposes amending the Criminal Code to achieve this goal:

“An individual article should be added to the Code to establish criminal liability for all forms of domestic violence. Alternatively, different chapters of the Code could include provisions covering specific forms of domestic violence, including beatings, psychological abuse, economic abuse, bodily harm, sexual violence and others.”

According to Anna Hakobyan, eradicating violence requires clear, realistic and effective legal mechanisms.

Before presenting the bill to parliament, she initiated discussions with independent experts and female MPs. Together, they plan to examine gaps in the existing legislation. Once the law comes into force, she has promised to launch the initiative’s second stage. This will involve:

organising an awareness campaign;

improving the skills of staff at relevant agencies;

ensuring the effective implementation of the new regulations.

“At the same time, a group of respected experts is preparing a nationwide study to collect the most accurate and comprehensive data possible on the prevalence of domestic violence against women in Armenia,” she said.

What preceded the campaign

This is not the prime minister’s wife’s first post about domestic violence. She has been actively raising the issue on her social media pages. At the end of July, she said she had received threats after a particular post, including threats to kill her.

“I hope the state authorities can prevent such a development, as it would seriously damage the country’s reputation if the prime minister’s wife became a victim of violence,” Hakobyan said.

At the same time, she urged women to overcome their fears and report cases of violence.

The Prosecutor General’s Office took note of her report. The Investigative Committee said it had opened a criminal case under the article on “hooliganism using information and communication technologies”.

“In addition, within the framework of another criminal case concerning public calls for violence, a warrant has been issued for the arrest of one person. The person has been placed on the wanted list,” Investigative Committee spokeswoman Kim Avdalyan said.

Statistics on domestic violence

The Investigative Committee said it opened 1,794 criminal cases related to domestic violence in the first half of 2026:

712 cases carried over from 2025;

1,082 cases opened in 2026.

Authorities sent 204 criminal cases to court and charged 213 people.

Of the 213 defendants in the cases sent to court, 150 were spouses of the victims, 20 were partners, 15 were parents or grandparents, five were brothers or sisters, 16 were children or grandchildren, one was the husband’s sister or brother, and six were sons- or daughters-in-law.

Of the 213 victims, 192 were over 18, while the rest were minors. Of those, 13 were under 12, three were aged 13-14, and five were aged 15-18.

Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

World.title: ‘Work is being carried out to international standards’ — Georgia’s Gelati Monastery Rehabilitation Committee responds to criticism
World.content:
Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati has described reports circulating on social media and in the media about conservation work at the monastery as disinformation.

The committee said the disinformation was harming efforts to restore Gelati.

The Gelati Monastery complex is one of Georgia’s most important medieval cultural and religious monuments. King David IV, known as David the Builder, founded it in 1106.

The complex’s main church is the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. In medieval Georgia, Gelati was not only a monastery but also an important centre of education and scholarship, home to the renowned Gelati Academy.

Recent reports and assessments have raised concerns about the condition of Gelati. The debate has focused on several issues:

The church’s temporary roof, which critics have called “cellophane”;

The risk of frescoes collapsing;

Mould and condensation inside the church;

The condition of the drainage system;

Plans to install an underfloor heating system;

Cooperation with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure;

The condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

What does the committee say?

The committee rejects claims that the Gelati Cathedral is covered with “cellophane”. According to the committee, the creation of a single temporary covering for the cathedral was one of the main requirements set by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre as early as 2020.

The committee says Georgian and German specialists jointly designed the roof. The authorities approved the project after considering several proposals. The covering uses a high-tech PVC-based material made in Germany specifically for Gelati. According to the committee, the material meets international conservation standards.

The committee also rejects reports of widespread loss of frescoes inside the cathedral. It says all critically damaged areas have been stabilised, while conservation work on the wall paintings is continuing in stages.

The statement also addresses Gelati’s historic drainage system. According to the committee, drainage channels built during the reign of David the Builder stopped functioning in 1510 after Ottoman forces burned the monastery. The committee says archaeological excavations also support this conclusion.

“For centuries, the drainage system was filled with earth, ash and coal,” the committee said.

The committee also responded to criticism over humidity and condensation inside the church. According to the committee, Italian professor Dario Camuffo conducted the study of Gelati’s microclimate. The committee considers him one of the recognised experts in the study of the microclimate of cultural heritage sites.

The committee explained that the problem at Gelati stems from the church’s massive walls, which retain the cold for a long time during winter. In spring, when outdoor temperatures rise and warm air enters the church, condensation can form on the walls and floor.

Camuffo suggested gradually heating the floor as one possible solution. However, the committee stressed that this remains a working hypothesis and requires further research before a final decision.

The committee also clarified the memorandum it signed with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure. According to the committee, the “pilot restoration” provided for in the document does not mean conducting experiments at Gelati. Instead, it refers to pilot or trial restoration work, which is standard international practice.

“This is a widely accepted standard for restoring wall paintings. Before treating an entire fresco, conservators test the safety of the proposed conservation methods on a small, less visible area. Only after obtaining a positive result do they begin the full-scale process,” the committee said.

In a significant part of its statement, the committee also responded to critics and addressed allegations about the condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

According to the committee, experts already knew about the poor condition of the mosaics in 1989. The claim is based on an assessment by restorer Carlo Bakuradze at the time, who found that about 85% of the mosaic depicting the Virgin Mary had detached from its base.

The committee also criticised specialists who question the ongoing conservation work and reminded them of their own responsibility for Gelati’s condition in the past.

“It is cynical and hypocritical for people to question the quality of conservation work when, under their direct supervision, extensive water-infiltration problems emerged within just one year at the recently built Bagrati Cathedral — problems that persist to this day,” the statement said. The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati urged critics not to try to damage the reputation of the ongoing work and to act according to professional ethics.

“We call on those pursuing certain subjective goals and agendas to refrain from attempts to discredit the conservation work carried out under the Gelati rehabilitation programme and deliberately mislead the public. We also call on them to return to the standards of common decency and professional ethics,” the committee said.

The committee concluded by stressing again that the work at the Gelati Monastery complex is unprecedented in scale, involves international experts and meets international conservation standards.

What happened at Gelati?

The main problem at Gelati Monastery is water and dampness, which have damaged the church’s wall paintings and mosaics over time. The situation became particularly serious after restoration work in recent years, including problems with the roof.

The problem became so serious that the UNESCO World Heritage Centre and its advisory bodies issued specific recommendations to Georgia. The authorities changed their approach to the restoration work in response to those recommendations and established the current Rehabilitation Committee.

A ruling by Georgia’s Supreme Court also notes that workers carried out roofing work at Gelati without an adequate expert assessment. The court found that problems with the materials used and the quality of the installation created a real risk of water entering the building.

Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

World.title: Suicides in Armenia’s military: the statistics and debate over who should be held responsible
World.content:
Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

In Armenia, debate continues over the causes of military deaths in peacetime and who should bear responsibility. A series of suicides has prompted the latest discussions. The first incident occurred on 21 July. Then, on 13 August, the Defence Ministry reported that it had found the body of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan with a gunshot wound. In both cases, the Investigative Committee said it had opened criminal proceedings under the article on negligent incitement to suicide.

According to the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, this was the 31st military death in Armenia in 2026. However, the Defence Ministry says 11 servicemen have died. Moreover, the ministry’s spokesperson said the number of military deaths had become the subject of various forms of manipulation.

“We often see reports in the press about 30 deaths in the army over the course of a year. But no one says how many of those 30 cases actually occurred in the army, which were related to military service and which were not. Even if the deaths were related to service, were all of them murders and suicides?” Aram Torosyan said, calling for greater precision.

Government bodies and civil society organisations also differ over who should bear responsibility for military deaths. Human rights groups tend to argue that the defence minister and the chief of the General Staff should be held accountable. However, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan does not share this view.

“In my assessment, it is not the case that the chief of the General Staff and the defence minister are failing to make sufficient efforts to address this issue,” Nikol Pashinyan said.

Civil society data differs from official figures

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan, who represents the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, said she had seen no positive changes. According to her, the number of military deaths in non-combat situations has not decreased:

“The situation is even worse than in 2025. There were 35 deaths throughout 2025, while there have already been 31 cases in the first eight months of this year.”

She stressed that 10 cases in 2025 were classified as related to military service, while the same number have been recorded in just eight months this year.

Defence Ministry spokesman Aram Torosyan says these claims do not match the official statistics.

“We have recorded 11 deaths this year. Only five of those who died were serving their mandatory military service. Some died from illness, while others died in a mine explosion,” he said.

Torosyan said six of the 11 deaths involved suicide or incitement to suicide, but only three were related to military service.

Commenting on last year’s figures, he stressed that there were no cases of murder in the army in 2025.

Causes of suicides in the army

The authorities have not released details about the death of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan. However, the prime minister said that 85-90% of suicides in the army result from:

gambling addiction and the debts it causes;

personal and family problems;

servicemen falling asleep while on duty, which can lead to conflicts with fellow soldiers.

“If a serviceman on duty at a border post falls asleep, he puts other people’s lives at risk. Soldiers then begin to treat the person who fell asleep at the post negatively, and he becomes isolated. After returning from combat duty, psychological pressure can also follow. We should not place all the blame on the army leadership. I am responsible for the fact that we have still not found a solution to this problem,” Pashinyan said.

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan believes that the first two causes mentioned by the prime minister have nothing to do with the army. At the same time, she believes authorities can eliminate the third factor by taking systemic measures:

“Why does a serviceman fall asleep while on duty? Are there enough personnel to ensure that everyone gets enough rest and does not feel the need to sleep while on duty?”

Prime minister’s statements and dismissals

On the day the soldier died, Nikol Pashinyan told reporters that the government had discussed the situation and decided to make dismissals. He announced personnel changes in the Military Police and the Defence Ministry’s Department of Moral and Psychological Support:

“We will analyse in detail why our efforts in this area are not producing the desired results and draw conclusions. Yes, there must be individual accountability.”

The same day, reports emerged that Military Police chief Ashot Zakaryan had submitted his resignation. Today, the president dismissed Zakaryan from the post he had held for six years. In another decree, Major General Aram Hovhannisyan was appointed to replace him. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy interior minister and police chief.

There are no specific details yet about personnel changes in the Department of Moral and Psychological Support.

In recent days, the Defence Ministry has reported consultations on organising psychological support in the armed forces. To review a report on the psychological assistance provided to the military, the defence minister met professors from Yerevan State University’s Research Centre for Psychology. The ministry is also holding discussions with conscript sergeants and officers serving on duty at military posts.

“The agenda includes issues related to preventing hazing and eliminating inappropriate behaviour in the army,” the ministry said.

Comment

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan believes:

“The army’s top command, led by Suren Papikyan, must give the public a detailed explanation of the series of deaths.

Has anyone from the army’s top command visited the military unit to establish the circumstances of the soldier’s death and find out what was happening there? I strongly doubt it.

Papikyan did not even visit the military unit in the village of Azat when 15 servicemen died.

On 19 January 2023, a fire broke out in the engineering and sapper company’s premises in the village of Azat, killing 15 servicemen. Three others suffered burns of varying severity.

Then, as now, Nikol Pashinyan spoke on Papikyan’s behalf. He named those responsible and accountable. But he did not explain what the Military Police had to do with the death.

If Pashinyan knows more about the situation in the army and at military units, why is Papikyan still the defence minister?”

Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

World.title: Emomali Rahmon reviews progress of tunnel construction at Rogun HPP
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon reviewed the progress of construction of transport tunnel No. 39 at the Rogun Hydropower Plant.

The information was announced by the press service of the President of Tajikistan.

The transport tunnel is designed to provide a connection between the right bank and the lower part of the Rogun HPP complex both during the construction period and after the plant is commissioned.

According to the project, the main tunnel is 2,192 meters long. It starts at an elevation of 1,320 meters and descends to 1,160 meters, where it reaches the lower section of the hydropower plant.

During the inspection, Rahmon was also presented with the project for an upper spillway tunnel with a length of 953 meters. Under the project, transport tunnel No. 39 will be connected to tunnel No. 23 and other underground structures of the complex.

The main purpose of the tunnel is to ensure the reliable movement of machinery, equipment, and construction materials, as well as to provide access to the facilities of the Rogun HPP.

Meanwhile, the Rogun Hydropower Plant is one of Tajikistan’s largest infrastructure projects and is being built on the Vakhsh River in the country’s east. The project envisages a total installed capacity of 3,780 MW and includes a large dam, underground tunnels and a network of supporting infrastructure.

Construction of the plant involves extensive underground works due to the mountainous terrain. Transport and auxiliary tunnels are being built to provide access to different sections of the complex, facilitate the movement of heavy machinery and materials, and support construction and future operation of the facility.

Once fully commissioned, Rogun HPP is expected to significantly increase Tajikistan’s electricity generation capacity and strengthen the reliability of its domestic power supply. The project is also intended to create additional potential for electricity exports to neighboring countries.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Saudi Arabia boost focus on trade and investment
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. Uzbekistan and Saudi Arabia are working to expand bilateral trade and investment ties.

This was reflected in a statement by the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, following a meeting between Minister Laziz Kudratov and Saad Abu Haimed, Saudi Arabia’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Uzbekistan, on August 20.

According to the Ministry, Saudi investments in Uzbekistan reached $2.8 billion in 2025, up 105% from a year earlier.

''Bilateral trade reached $178 million in 2025, an increase of 24% year over year. Uzbekistan currently has 433 enterprises with Saudi capital participation,'' the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade notes.

The sides focused on increasing and diversifying bilateral trade, organizing business missions and exhibitions, and advancing joint projects across several sectors.

Priority areas include energy, digital technologies, transport, finance, healthcare and education, according to the ministry.

''Uzbekistan and Saudi Arabia are placing particular emphasis on expanding trade, strengthening investment cooperation and advancing joint projects in priority sectors,'' the ministry said.

The sides also discussed increasing direct business contacts through reciprocal business missions and participation in exhibitions, which could help companies identify new commercial and investment opportunities.

Saudi investment has become an increasingly important component of Uzbekistan’s economic cooperation with the Gulf country. The 105% annual increase in utilized Saudi investment highlights the expansion of the two countries’ investment ties.

Following the meeting, Uzbekistan proposed holding the next meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission in Riyadh in the fourth quarter of 2026.

The parties also discussed arrangements for Uzbekistan’s participation in EXPO 2030 in Saudi Arabia, including the establishment of an Uzbekistan national pavilion.

The planned commission meeting is expected to provide an additional platform for reviewing bilateral economic projects and identifying new areas for cooperation.

The latest discussions reflect Tashkent’s efforts to deepen economic ties with Saudi Arabia through greater trade diversification, investment, and business-to-business cooperation.

World.title: Azerbaijan sees sharp increase in primary market transactions in Q2 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. Azerbaijan recorded changes in the number and value of primary and secondary stock market transactions in the second quarter of 2026.

This was stated in the Statistical Bulletin for the first and second quarters of 2026 published by the National Depository Center.

According to the bulletin, the number of primary stock market transactions denominated in Azerbaijani manats reached 21,919 in the second quarter, with a total value of $539.5 million. In the first quarter, the figures stood at 1,245 transactions and $245.8 million, respectively.

Thus, the number of primary market transactions in manats increased by 20,674, while their total value rose by $293.7 million compared with the first quarter.

The number of primary stock market transactions denominated in US dollars stood at 106 in the second quarter, with a total value of $5 million. In the first quarter, there were 104 transactions worth $2 million.

On the secondary market, the number of transactions in manats reached 5,533 in the second quarter, with a total value of $81.4 million, compared with 3,031 transactions worth $370.0 million in the first quarter.

Thus, the number of secondary market transactions in manats increased by 2,502, while their total value decreased by $288.6 million compared with the previous quarter.

The number of secondary stock market transactions in US dollars reached 275 in the second quarter, with a total value of $41.04 million. In the first quarter, there were 199 transactions worth $29.97 million.

Thus, the number of dollar-denominated secondary market transactions increased by 76, while their total value rose by $11.07 million in the second quarter.
