World.title: Uzbekistan Railways advances tariff reform with World Bank support
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. “Uzbekistan Railways” is advancing work on a new tariff-setting methodology as part of broader reforms of the country's railway sector, in collaboration with international consultants and the World Bank, along with relevant government agencies.

This was stated by Uzbekistan Railways following a working meeting attended by international consultants engaged with the support of the World Bank, as well as specialists from relevant ministries and government agencies.

The meeting is part of Uzbekistan’s ongoing railway sector transformation under a presidential resolution adopted in October 2023 on fundamental reforms in the railway transport sector and a December 2024 directive aimed at accelerating the sector’s transformation.

During the meeting, participants reviewed final proposals for a new tariff methodology prepared with the support of the World Bank and input from local experts.

The proposed methodology is designed to introduce transparent mechanisms for setting transport service prices, improve the efficiency of infrastructure use and create more favorable conditions for attracting foreign investment.

“The main objective of the new methodology is to transform the railway system into an economically independent and competitive sector,” Uzbekistan Railways said.

Participants exchanged views on the proposed approach and assessed ways to improve the efficiency and financial sustainability of railway operations.

The new tariff framework is expected to provide clearer principles for pricing transport services while supporting more efficient use of railway infrastructure.

The reform could also help create a more predictable environment for investors and operators by making tariff-setting mechanisms more transparent and consistent.

Following a detailed review of the agenda, participants identified the next practical steps for refining the document based on the proposals raised during the meeting.

The expert group agreed to accelerate work to finalize the tariff methodology and submit it for approval in the near term.

The initiative forms part of Uzbekistan’s broader efforts to transform the railway sector, strengthen its competitiveness and improve the economic efficiency of the country’s rail transport system.

World.title: Azerbaijan plans daily, weekly, monthly rail ticket packages for tourists
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. Azerbaijan plans to introduce daily, weekly and monthly railway ticket packages for tourists, as well as discounted ticket offers for specific destinations, by 2030.

This is outlined in the State Program for Tourism Development for 2026–2030, approved by President Ilham Aliyev today.

The Ministry of Digital Development and Transport has been tasked with taking measures in this area.

As a first step, international practices in this field will be studied.

World.title: North Korea fires missiles into sea as South Korea, US hold military drills
World.content:
North Korea has fired several short-range ballistic missiles into the sea, according to South Korea's military, a day after Seoul announced it was scaling back its military drills with the United States.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff said about 10 short-range ballistic missiles were launched from Pyongyang towards North Korea's eastern waters at around 5pm local time on Thursday.

South Korea's presidential national security council held an emergency meeting following the missile launches and issued a statement urging North Korea to halt ballistic missile launches that are banned by UN Security Council resolutions.

South Korea has since bolstered its surveillance posture and said it was closely coordinating information with the United States and Japan.

The Japanese prime minister's office also confirmed it had detected a suspected missile launch.

South Korea has reduced its training drills with the United States from 11 days to five. (AP: Ahn Young-joon)

The missile launch comes amid the US and South Korea's annual military training drills and less than a day after US President Donald Trump said he planned to meet North Korea leader Kim Jong Un later this year.

Trump says he will meet North Korea's Kim Jong Un later this year The US president made the announcement days after ordering the US scale back its military drills with South Korea.

The training drills will end six days early this year after Mr Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back the exercise.

The Ulchi Freedom Shield is one of the main military exercises conducted by the US and South Korea each year to enhance their ability to cope with potential North Korean aggression.

While Washington and Seoul say their drills are defensive in nature, North Korea calls them an invasion rehearsal and often reacts with weapons tests.

Before this month's drills started, North Korea accused the US and South Korea of plotting more provocative exercises this summer and vowed to respond with "a new level of a deterrent".

China weighs in on Korean Peninsula tensions

South Korean National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac meets with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Seoul. (Yonhap via Reuters)

Thursday's missile launch also came as China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited South Korea.

During the visit, the foreign minister urged South Korea not to take sides between Beijing and Washington, saying the US should abandon its "hostile" policy towards North Korea to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

"The fundamental solution to the tensions on the Korean Peninsula lies in addressing the root causes of the problem and urging the United States to abandon its hostile policy toward North Korea," he said, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, during a meeting with South Korea's National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac.

China hopes South Korea will "achieve genuine strategic autonomy, refrain from bloc confrontation and taking sides, and develop relations with major powers including China and the United States in parallel and without contradiction".

North Korea also fired a short-range ballistic missile over the Sea of Japan earlier this month, a day after Pyongyang criticised Japan's military build-up in the region.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Russian missile strikes kill 13 in Kyiv, more than 30 injured
World.content:
Russian ballistic missiles have killed at least 13 people and injured more than 30 in Kyiv, authorities say, damaging buildings and severing power supply to some parts of the Ukrainian capital.

A fire broke out, and the upper floors of a nine-storey residential block were destroyed in the city's Solomianskyi district, where seven people were killed, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, calling for Friday to be observed as a day of mourning.

Two other districts also suffered damage, Mr Klitschko said on the Telegram messaging app, with non-residential facilities, warehouses, a school and a children's hospital hit.

Power company DTEK said it restored electricity to more than half of the roughly 90,000 homes left without power in the capital following the attack.

Russia has intensified its air strikes on Ukraine over the summer. (Reuters: Anatolii Stepanov)

"There used to be a building here, and now it's gone," said 45-year-old resident Maria Abramova.

She had only just reached her children's room after the air raid alert sounded when explosions rang out, blowing her windows out and "nearly killing" her husband.

Russia has stepped up air strikes on Ukraine in recent months, trying to exploit its smaller neighbour's critical shortage of interceptors to down ballistic missiles.

The Russian defence ministry said Moscow attacked Kyiv and the surrounding region with air strikes and drones, hitting facilities producing drone components, a military depot and a logistics hub, as well as other targets.

A woman in Kyiv reacts after finding out her grandson has died in the Russian attacks. (Reuters: Anatolii Stepanov)

A resident reported hearing more than a dozen explosions. In the region around the Ukrainian capital, another person was killed, an official said on Telegram.

Ukraine's emergency service showed video of servicemen battling a blaze in a building and helping people to escape facilities destroyed during the night in Kyiv.

Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

Smoke rises from a food warehouse hit by a Russian missile strike near Kyiv. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Diplomatic efforts have failed so far to yield a lasting ceasefire in the war, which started with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Russian bank fires economist Andrei Klepach, one of Russia's most prominent macroeconomists, has predicted a social crisis and says costs are "mounting" over the Ukraine war.

A drone crashed into NATO and European Union member Romania during the Russian attack on Ukraine, the Romanian defence ministry said on Thursday. A drone also crossed Moldova's airspace, the country's military said.

Ukraine had handed proposals to US negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, for a plan to end the war, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said this month, and he has also repeatedly asked for interceptor missiles to ward off missile attacks.

Russia did not receive specific proposals for possible new meetings with US negotiators, foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the Izvestia newspaper.

But she added that Moscow would be ready to arrange a meeting at short notice.

Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner were last in Moscow last January and have not yet visited Kyiv.

Wires/ABC

World.title: 'Is this accurate?' How one note magnified the tragedy of bushwalker's family
World.content:
"Is this accurate?"

That was the immediate reaction of New South Wales Premier Chris Minns when he was passed a note in parliament shortly before midday.

He had already faced two hours of questioning in a budget estimates hearing and still had another hour to go.

The note was a surprising, but welcome distraction from questions about uranium mining.

After being assured the information was credible, the premier made an announcement that brought joy to the room.

"We've got some fantastic news, Mr Chair," he said.

"Lily Hooper has been found alive."

The NSW premier was handed the note during budget estimates. (ABC News)

There were murmurs of relief from MPs, many of whom had been following the news about the missing 18-year-old hiker.

Ms Hooper left her home south-west of Sydney on the morning of Wednesday, August 12, to go hiking in the Nattai National Park.

Her car was later found near the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, sparking a large-scale multi-agency search involving nearly 1,000 people, according to police.

The premier went on to thank the police, the State Emergency Service (SES), defence personnel and the many others who had joined the search.

It was a moment of levity in a sometimes combative hearing.

The premier's announcement was widely reported, including by the ABC.

About 25 minutes later, the premier was handed another note, containing the worst possible news.

A tragic miscommunication

Lily Hooper's body was found after an eight-day search. (Supplied: NSW Police)

By that stage, the hearing had resumed normal programming, with opposition MP Natalie Ward asking a series of pointed questions about the office of local government.

After conferring with Secretary of the Cabinet Office, Kate Boyd, a stony-faced Mr Minns made another announcement.

"I've got some terrible news," he said.

"I apologise to the committee, but it seems as if the early advice was wrong.

"Lily's body's been found, and she's been found deceased."

"Oh my god," replied committee chair Jeremy Buckingham.

Members of the Australia Defence Force also joined the search. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The premier continued.

"I only raise that because I made the earlier advice and I'm very sorry for that," he said.

"This is obviously devastating, and I'm just profoundly sad for her family and all those concerned."

Police said about 11:30am a body believed to be that of Ms Hooper was located in bushland.

The premier's anguish was plain to see.

Not only had he been provided with incorrect information, but his earlier statement had brought the community an immense sense of relief that was abruptly snatched away.

People would be entitled to wonder how such an error could be made.

It soon became clear the miscommunication occurred much further down the chain.

Unfortunately, it made its way to the top before anyone could stop it.

The error fuelled by 'elation'

The NSW assistant police commissioner said there was a delay in effectively communicating the fact that Lily Hooper had died. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Speaking to reporters in the Southern Highlands, NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Joseph Cassar pointed to the communication challenges search teams were facing using handheld radios.

An SES volunteer made the initial discovery and was following protocol by reporting it up, he said.

However, he said there was a delay in effectively communicating the fact that Ms Hooper had died.

During the intervening period of between eight and 10 minutes, Ms Hooper's family, who were in close contact with the police, were led to believe she was alive.

Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon apologised "unreservedly" to the family.

"The miscommunication obviously was born out of elation that Lily had been found, and her condition at that time was such that searchers were relieved," he said.

"Certainly, those at the command post were elated.

"Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously we know now the impact on her family."

By that stage, the initial report of Ms Hooper having been found had already found its way to the government.

Police have well-established lines of communication into the offices of both the premier and the police minister, Yasmin Catley.

Word travels fast, by necessity.

During media conferences or Question Time, both are regularly asked for updates on police investigations or emergency operations, so they need to be well-briefed.

A large-scale multi-agency search was launched. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Just as the public is right to expect that the information the premier provides is accurate, he is right to expect the information being passed up the chain is correct.

The commissioner said the incorrect report was passed via police commands into the offices of both the premier and the police minister.

While he "wasn't given notice" of the premier's announcement, he was not surprised that he had made it.

"When Lily was located, obviously there was elation," Commissioner Lanyon said.

"That information got passed through very quickly.

"It's unsurprising that it went quickly up into government."

Police have now committed to reviewing and improving their communication on the ground, particularly when working with the SES.

It is also likely to prompt some rebalancing between the speed and accuracy of the information they provide to the government, which today showed how quickly it can disseminate it.

On this occasion, that balance was off, magnifying both a mistake and a family's tragedy.

World.title: 'Completely unacceptable': Albanese lashes AFL over response to Swans scandal
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has criticised the AFL over its handling of the current scandal engulfing the league.

On Wednesday, the Swans stood down five players for the rest of the AFL season — vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey — for breaching club standards for drinking and bringing women to the hotel.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad have since flown to New South Wales and are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Swans players James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey and Riley Bice have been stood down. (Getty Images/ABC News)

Mr Albanese told 7.30 that he felt the initial response was not good enough.

"It's extraordinary that this has occurred," Mr Albanese said.

"The idea that this is occurring is completely untenable, and the initial response as well was, I think, completely unacceptable.

"The NRL have a no-fault stand down clause for issues like this, but the first thoughts should have been always about women and their safety.

" I don't think that occurred at this time. The AFL certainly needs to do better. "

That initial response came on Monday afternoon when Swans CEO and Fremantle Dockers great Matthew Pavlich confirmed several players had been linked to the alleged incident.

Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich has issued several statements this week. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing," Mr Pavlich said on Monday.

"But safe to say that we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation."

On Tuesday AFL CEO Andrew Dillon described the allegations as "deeply disturbing" in a statement.

On Thursday night the ABC reported that detectives investigating have been told some players paid female adult entertainers to consume drugs off their bodies.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mr Albanese said the AFL and the Swans should "have a good look" at their culture.

Albanese to press Israel over Frankcom

While Mr Albanese was focused on several issues at home, the major geopolitical issue of the day involved Israel.

On Wednesday night, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing over a 2024 strike on a humanitarian convoy, which killed Australian woman Zomi Frankcom.

Ms Frankcom was killed in a strike by the IDF. (Supplied: Facebook)

The decision was described as an "outrage" by Foreign Minister Penny Wong on Thursday morning.

Mr Albanese told 7.30 he wanted a much more transparent response from the Israeli government.

"It clearly is an outrage and there's a need for a far more transparent and clear explanation from the Israeli government other than what we've received," Mr Albanese said.

Asked if that would involve an independent investigation, Mr Albanese said it was one option.

"It's certainly not good enough that on World Humanitarian Day ... they release this so-called report that essentially says, 'Yes, we're responsible, but nothing to see here', he said".

"Zomi represented the best of Australians out there in a dangerous area, helping her fellow global citizens as she had in other parts of the world that were suffering conflict as well. And that's why it deserves better.

"Her family deserved better, and frankly, Australia deserves better.

"We will press the Israeli government.

"[We] will discuss with Ms Frankcom's family. They deserve to be consulted on these issues and we'll do that, and then we'll make an announcement in coming days."

PM concedes podcast appearance was 'an error'

The Prime Minister was also asked about criticism he's faced over several comments he made on the Deep Bush podcast.

Loading...

Mr Albanese first came under scrutiny for playing "shag, marry, date" on the podcast, which was broadcast in July.

He has since unequivocally apologised for saying he would "shag" Kylie Minogue.

Recently it was hand gestures he made on the podcast, while referring to a pair of melons given to him by Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, that caused controversy.

Mr Albanese has not apologised specifically for the melon interaction and maintains that the gestures have been misinterpreted.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

However, he told 7.30 that in hindsight he should not have gone on the podcast and that he had learned from it.

"I learned that I need to do better every day," Mr Albanese said.

"If I had my time again ... then I wouldn't have done that podcast.

" We have a view which is trying to talk to as many people as possible, but clearly that was an error. "

World.title: Zomi Frankcom's family 'deeply disappointed' IDF won't pursue charges
World.content:
The family of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, who was killed in an Israeli strike while delivering humanitarian aid in Gaza in 2024, has slammed the Israeli military's decision not to pursue criminal charges against the commanders who ordered the attack.

The statement, issued by Zomi's brother Mal on behalf of the Frankcom family, said family members were "deeply disappointed" by the decision, having spent the past two years waiting for justice while "hoping and calling for an independent criminal investigation".

"Zomi and her colleagues deserve more than an internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing," they said.

" The families of the victims deserve transparency and an independent judicial assessment of the criminal responsibility for the international humanitarian law violations that took place on that day. "

Ms Frankcom was one of seven World Central Kitchen aid workers killed on April 1, 2024, while taking part in a convoy helping to deliver food and other supplies to northern Gaza.

The group was travelling in three armoured cars branded with the World Central Kitchen logo, and driving through part of the Gaza Strip that had been declared a "humanitarian fire control zone" while coordinating movements with the IDF (Israel Defense Forces).

An Israeli drone fired three missiles at the convoy — one at each of the cars in succession — as survivors of the initial strike attempted to move from one vehicle to another.

Wreckage of one of three World Central Kitchen vehicles destroyed in the strikes. (Reuters: Ahmed Zakot)

An Australian investigation into the Israeli government's response to the incident, led by retired defence chief Air Chief Marshal Mark Binskin, found the deaths had been the result of the first vehicle being misidentified due to a number of factors, including the presence of armed security in the vicinity, confirmation bias and a "failure within the IDF to fully disseminate and/or read the detailed movement plan approved by the convoy".

Wong declares 'difficult time' in relations with Israel Foreign Minister Penny Wong says she has "no confidence" in the IDF investigation that cleared Israeli soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.

The subsequent strikes were also found to be a breach of IDF procedures and the rules of engagement, echoing the findings of a rapid FFAM ("fact-finding and assessment mechanism") investigation conducted by the IDF in the days following the incident.

Two IDF officers were fired in the weeks after the strikes, while others were reprimanded.

In their statement released on Thursday evening, Ms Frankcom's family expressed disagreement with the finding that there was no wrongdoing involved that merited at least a criminal investigation, highlighting the follow-up strikes as well as the fact that one of the officers involved had reportedly signed a letter earlier that year calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.

They also expressed outrage at the timing of the announcement, which came on World Humanitarian Day, an internationally recognised day dedicated to those who have died working for humanitarian causes.

A humanitarian award has since been created in Ms Frankcom's name. (Supplied: X)

The family had been standing alongside Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong at an event at Parliament House just hours prior to the announcement, launching a humanitarian award in Ms Frankcom's name.

"For it to be announced on World Humanitarian Day, the day the world pauses to remember those who have lost their lives while helping others … is an insult to my sister's memory," Ms Frankcom's brother Mal said.

Senator Wong similarly expressed anger at the announcement, saying she had no confidence in the IDF's findings, and calling in Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, to explain the decision.

Calling today's events a "difficult time" in diplomatic relations with Israel, she said she was informed of the IDF's decision just minutes before it was publicly announced, and did not have time to alert Ms Frankcom's family.

World.title: Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning
World.content:
The Penrith Panthers have held on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

The Panthers shot out to a 22-0 lead courtesy of a Brian To'o hat-trick and Liam Henry try, but did not score again after the half-hour mark.

Back rower Liam Martin was sent to the sin-bin for a professional foul shortly before half-time and Penrith was Lindsay Smith was binned just after the break for repeated ruck infringements.

Melbourne managed to get on the board against 11 men when Tyran Wishart skipped through the teeth of the defence, and Jack Howarth put a move on Izack Tago to crash over soon after Smith returned to the field.

Jack Cogger joined the list of sin-binned players, which also included Storm back rower Oryn Keeley from the first half, when he hit Wishart high, leading to Siulagi Tuimalatu-Brown's try on the right wing.

But wayward kicking by Nick Meaney and some attacking miscues kept the Storm from getting too close as they fell out of the finals race for the first time since 2010, when they played for no points due to salary cap infringements.

Prior to that, the Storm have not missed the finals since 2002, before Craig Bellamy took over as coach.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Proposed gun reforms 'betrayal of Tasmanians', critics say
World.content:
The Tasmanian government's watered-down gun law reforms have been described as "extraordinarily weak" and a "betrayal of Tasmanians" by Labor and the Greens.

The proposed reforms, which were tabled in state parliament on Thursday, were a response to calls to tighten gun laws in the wake of last year's Bondi terror attack.

But gun control advocates say the legislation tabled today is even "weaker" than the much-criticised draft legislation released earlier this year.

The bill still does not include a limit on the number of guns one person can own, despite the state's Police Commissioner Donna Adams calling for it.

It still reclassifies straight pull and button or lever release shotguns to the more restrictive Category C and introduces an Australian citizenship requirement for owners, with carve-outs for New Zealand citizens and people who need them for work.

But it now grandfathers these clauses, meaning the rules do not apply to guns that people already own or to non-citizens who currently own legal guns.

One gun advocate says "law-abiding firearms owners probably aren't going to be too happy" with the reforms. (ABC News)

Greens' police spokesperson Tabatha Badger said the bill was "deeply disappointing" and "simply not good enough".

"Tasmanians expected so much more when it came to firearm safety in this state," she said.

"We'd already seen a draft bill out for public consultation that was underwhelming, and what we've seen today tabled in this parliament is an incredible disappointment.

"It's very clear that this police minister does not understand that public safety is a core part of his job."

Tabatha Badger says the government should be "incredibly ashamed" of its proposal. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Ms Badger cited the Port Arthur shootings of 1996 and raised concerns about the grandfathering of clauses, the decision to include changes to antique gun laws and the addition of mandatory minimum sentences for stolen firearms.

"This Liberal government should be incredibly ashamed of what they have put forward," she said.

"Tasmania was a state that, in the past, has led the way off the back of incredible tragedy to reform firearms to help make our community safer. In the years that have followed, we simply haven't kept up with that."

What we know about guns in Australia Gun control researchers say we have "no idea" how many black market and 3D-printed weapons are out there.

Labor leader Josh Willie accused the government of being "soft on crime".

"This is a betrayal of Tasmanians and community safety by Premier Rockliff," he said.

"He has a position to support unlimited guns.

" He's backflipped on his position to improve community safety and I think, rightly, Tasmanians will be questioning whether he's got their back. "

Bill defended by police minister

The bill also follows through on a 2024 election promise of no licence requirements for antique firearms.

Antique firearms manufactured before January 1, 1900 will only have to be registered with Tasmania Police.

Police Minister Felix Ellis said the legislation strikes the right balance and will result in a significant uplift in community safety.

Police Minister Felix Ellis has defended the changes, saying Tasmanians will be safer as a result of the reforms. (Facebook: Felix Ellis)

He defended the grandfathered clauses, saying they were about "ensuring that the transition is right".

"That we can continue to support people who are farmers, hunters and recreational shooters who have been complying with the law," he said.

"We had people who have lived here for decades, who are not citizens of Australia, but have complied with our laws here in Tasmania when it comes to their firearms and [are of] good character, so rather than unduly penalising those people, it allows us to establish a framework moving forward."

Mr Ellis also said the mandatory minimum sentences for stolen firearms were particularly important.

"It'll ensure that if you steal a firearm or you're caught in possession of a stolen firearm you will go to jail," he said.

"That is absolutely vital so we can ensure that illegal firearms are not being used to intimidate our community and aren't being used to fuel organised crime."

An agreement to reclassify guns has been grandfathered, prompting backlash. (ABC News)

The bill will support the implementation of the National Firearms Register in the state, which the minister said would improve intelligence sharing between law enforcement and intelligence agencies.

"We've seen that the failures of Bondi have been very much about the failure to share intelligence, particularly about people who are seeking to do harm in the community," Mr Ellis said.

"So this uplift will be critical."

Opposition to push amendments

Gun Control Australia vice president Roland Browne accused the Tasmanian government of going sideways and backwards.

"The agreement reached in December required reclassification of guns and Tasmania has done that, but then they've grandfathered the clauses that make those reclassification decisions operative.

"In other words, if people are going to have their guns reclassified … shooters in Tasmania keep their guns.

" How is that going to make Tasmania a safer place? "

Roland Browne questions the efficacy of the proposed reforms. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

But nor were gun advocates satisfied.

In a social media video, Tasmanian Shooters Union President Phillip Bigg said it didn't seem like their consultations were taken note of.

"Law-abiding firearms owners probably aren't going to be too happy," he said.

"I've had a quick look, doesn't look very good."

Mr Bigg also acknowledged that Labor and the Greens were likely to try to make their own amendments to the bill.

That was confirmed by both parties today, with Mr Willie telling the media the party is still intent on introducing caps on guns.

"We've said consistently we'll promote community safety while respecting the legitimate ownership of legal firearms owners," he said.

"We'll work with the parliament around amendments. We're committed to doing that."

Phillip Bigg says the Tasmanian Shooters Union would work with parliament on the amendments. (ABC News)

The two parties combined will need to find another four votes to get any amendments through the lower house.

The state government said there will be a six-month voluntary buyback scheme that will begin once the bill has royal assent.

It is still in negotiations with the federal government about the cost.

Parliament is set to debate the bill in the first week of September.

A Perth father has died after allegedly being attacked by a group of Australians while on holiday in Bali. Paul Dougan, from Gosnells, underwent three surgeries, including to have his spleen removed, after the attack 10 days ago. Paul Dougan has died after allegedly being set upon by a group of Aussies in a Bali bar 10 days ago. He was on a trip with friends when he was allegedly assaulted at One Tribe bar in Kuta by a group of strangers, believed to be Australian, after his friends had left to go home. “To have this happen to him, of all people, is just devastating,” friend David Coughtrie told 9News Perth.



“He’s not the kind of guy to go looking for that sort of trouble. “He’d grabbed his partner and said, ‘Let’s get out of here’. As he stood up he was confronted by a person that said, ‘What did you say?’ and pretty much didn’t wait for an answer and just struck him.” Perth father Paul Dougan has been hospitalised in Bali after allegedly being assaulted by fellow Australians while on holiday. GoFundMe Dougan’s injuries included 10 broken ribs and severe internal bleeding. His family rushed to Bali to be with him and on Wednesday his son Liam launched a GoFundMe page to help pay for mounting medical costs.



But as donations started pouring in, Dougan lost his battle while in intensive care. Related Article Inquest Behind bars for 30 years, out for 79 days: Perth inquest probes complex final months of a killer Liam posted to social media saying, “it wasn’t meant to be this way Dad”, adding, “I will love and remember you for the rest of my life and I will continue to make you proud. “I am shattered, lost, heartbroken and confused but grateful I ever got to call you my Dad,” the post, made on Thursday evening, read. Liam had earlier made a video explaining what had happened and how Indonesian police were in the process of trying to track down those responsible.



“It looks to be a group of four of the suspects that we’ve got and [they were] beating him heavily while on the floor,” he said. On the fundraising page, Liam wrote his father was “brutally assaulted by a group of Australians who are yet to be identified”. “They beat and kicked him multiple times putting him in a life-threatening condition,” it read. “From this Paul suffered internal bleeding and 10 broken ribs, has undergone three major surgeries, had his spleen removed, required four blood transfusions, and currently has drains in both his lungs and abdomen as a result of the internal injuries and bleeding from the attack. “He has now been in ICU for 10 days and remains sedated following his third surgery.”



On Thursday evening the fundraiser had received more than $45,000 in donations. With 9News Perth

World.title: Swill waters run deep
World.content:
“Apropos David Sayers’ soft drink saga (C8), in my teens, I worked at the local lolly water factory in Muswellbrook in the holidays,” writes Denis Cartledge of Tenterfield. “It was a Friday afternoon event for one particular worker to be thrown in the softwater tank that supplied the factory. He rarely washed, and his workmates thought they’d help his cleanliness regime. Looking back, I don’t think the tank was drained, cleaned and/or refilled. It was around that time we decided to stop buying a mixed crate of lolly water every few months.”

The current dress code discussion (C8) is revealing a few workarounds. Here’s Bev Matthews of Wallerawang: “Back in the early ’80s, three friends and I tried to get into a club in Parramatta. One of the boys had a collarless shirt on, and they wouldn’t let him in. I happened to be wearing a knitted cardigan with a collar (like I said, it was the ’80s). He donned it, and voilà, they let him in.”

“In the late 1970s, my brother-in-law went for an after work beer at the Manly Yacht Club in Brisbane, of which he was a member,” says Colleen Riga of Potts Point. “Clad in his work gear consisting of boots, stubbies and polo shirt, he was told that club rules required a tie for evening entry. They had no problem with the work gear, so, looking through a box under the counter containing ‘emergency neckwear’ they presented him with a clip-on bow-tie (or ‘blowfly’ as he incorrectly heard) and he was free to enjoy a coldie.”

Reading about Mash McDonald’s in Iran (C8) reminded Ann MacKenzie of St Ives of the time she was in Tehran in 2017 and noticed a fast food establishment dubbed ZFC.

In reply to Stephen Tait’s inquiry into the wellbeing of Dirranbandi pubsters the Norton Brothers (C8), Janice Creenaune of Austinmer says the visit was earlier in the year, on Anzac Day in fact, and that the pub was “heaving with 2-up patrons. However, today we are off to camp near the ‘Hog and Billy’ in Girilambone, (known colloquially as ‘Girl’ I believe). Is there anybody we can look up for you there, Stephen?”

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese opposite Nikki Osborne on the Bush Deep podcast which aired in July. Bush Deep Podcast “We have a view which is trying to talk to as many people as possible, but clearly, that was an error,” Albanese said. The prime minister’s appearance opposite Nikki Osborne on an episode of the Bush Deep podcast, which aired in early July, spawned some uproars.



The first came over a game of “marry, date, shag” when he nominated pop star Kylie Minogue for “all of the above”. He subsequently apologised, facing heavy criticism from political opponents saying he had demonstrated a lack of judgment and should have known better than to play along with the inappropriate game. But the controversy escalated as parliament returned earlier in August, when Japan’s former ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami wrote in The Australian that Albanese made an “insulting” gesture while talking about crown melons gifted to him by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in May. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese accepts a Shizuoka crown melon from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Canberra in May. x.com/takaichi_sanae During the podcast, filmed at The Lodge, Osborne joked to Albanese about Takaichi smuggling the crown melons under her shirt “like Pamela Anderson”. Albanese then gestured with both hands as he told Osborne the gift had been “a couple of melons”. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi appeared at a press conference alongside Australian counterpart Richard Marles in Canberra this week, playing down the controversy.

World.title: Perth dad dies after allegedly being attacked by ‘group of Aussies’ in a Bali bar
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth dad dies after allegedly being attacked by ‘group of Aussies’ in a Bali bar Rebecca Peppiatt and Amber Wilkinson August 20, 2026 — 9:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth father has died after allegedly being attacked by a group of Australians while on holiday in Bali. Paul Dougan, from Gosnells, underwent three surgeries, including to have his spleen removed, after the attack 10 days ago. Paul Dougan has died after allegedly being set upon by a group of Aussies in a Bali bar 10 days ago. He was on a trip with friends when he was allegedly assaulted at One Tribe bar in Kuta by a group of strangers, believed to be Australian, after his friends had left to go home. “To have this happen to him, of all people, is just devastating,” friend David Coughtrie told 9News Perth.



“He’s not the kind of guy to go looking for that sort of trouble. “He’d grabbed his partner and said, ‘Let’s get out of here’. As he stood up he was confronted by a person that said, ‘What did you say?’ and pretty much didn’t wait for an answer and just struck him.” Perth father Paul Dougan has been hospitalised in Bali after allegedly being assaulted by fellow Australians while on holiday. GoFundMe Dougan’s injuries included 10 broken ribs and severe internal bleeding. His family rushed to Bali to be with him and on Wednesday his son Liam launched a GoFundMe page to help pay for mounting medical costs.



But as donations started pouring in, Dougan lost his battle while in intensive care. Related Article Inquest Behind bars for 30 years, out for 79 days: Perth inquest probes complex final months of a killer Liam posted to social media saying, “it wasn’t meant to be this way Dad”, adding, “I will love and remember you for the rest of my life and I will continue to make you proud. “I am shattered, lost, heartbroken and confused but grateful I ever got to call you my Dad,” the post, made on Thursday evening, read. Liam had earlier made a video explaining what had happened and how Indonesian police were in the process of trying to track down those responsible.



“It looks to be a group of four of the suspects that we’ve got and [they were] beating him heavily while on the floor,” he said. On the fundraising page, Liam wrote his father was “brutally assaulted by a group of Australians who are yet to be identified”. “They beat and kicked him multiple times putting him in a life-threatening condition,” it read. “From this Paul suffered internal bleeding and 10 broken ribs, has undergone three major surgeries, had his spleen removed, required four blood transfusions, and currently has drains in both his lungs and abdomen as a result of the internal injuries and bleeding from the attack. “He has now been in ICU for 10 days and remains sedated following his third surgery.”



On Thursday evening the fundraiser had received more than $45,000 in donations. With 9News Perth

World.title: Swill waters run deep
World.content:
“Apropos David Sayers’ soft drink saga (C8), in my teens, I worked at the local lolly water factory in Muswellbrook in the holidays,” writes Denis Cartledge of Tenterfield. “It was a Friday afternoon event for one particular worker to be thrown in the softwater tank that supplied the factory. He rarely washed, and his workmates thought they’d help his cleanliness regime. Looking back, I don’t think the tank was drained, cleaned and/or refilled. It was around that time we decided to stop buying a mixed crate of lolly water every few months.”

The current dress code discussion (C8) is revealing a few workarounds. Here’s Bev Matthews of Wallerawang: “Back in the early ’80s, three friends and I tried to get into a club in Parramatta. One of the boys had a collarless shirt on, and they wouldn’t let him in. I happened to be wearing a knitted cardigan with a collar (like I said, it was the ’80s). He donned it, and voilà, they let him in.”

“In the late 1970s, my brother-in-law went for an after work beer at the Manly Yacht Club in Brisbane, of which he was a member,” says Colleen Riga of Potts Point. “Clad in his work gear consisting of boots, stubbies and polo shirt, he was told that club rules required a tie for evening entry. They had no problem with the work gear, so, looking through a box under the counter containing ‘emergency neckwear’ they presented him with a clip-on bow-tie (or ‘blowfly’ as he incorrectly heard) and he was free to enjoy a coldie.”

Reading about Mash McDonald’s in Iran (C8) reminded Ann MacKenzie of St Ives of the time she was in Tehran in 2017 and noticed a fast food establishment dubbed ZFC.

In reply to Stephen Tait’s inquiry into the wellbeing of Dirranbandi pubsters the Norton Brothers (C8), Janice Creenaune of Austinmer says the visit was earlier in the year, on Anzac Day in fact, and that the pub was “heaving with 2-up patrons. However, today we are off to camp near the ‘Hog and Billy’ in Girilambone, (known colloquially as ‘Girl’ I believe). Is there anybody we can look up for you there, Stephen?”

World.title: Big names back for All Blacks as team to play Springboks revealed
World.content:
The All Blacks have recalled several star players with Cam Roigard, Will Jordan and Damian McKenzie named to start in this weekend's test against the Springboks in Johannesburg.

The trio return from injury to take their place in the side while Ardie Savea resumes the captaincy duties after being rested for the first three games of the South African tour.

Savea is at No.8 with coach Dave Rennie retaining the loose forward trio from last month's win against Ireland, with Luke Jacobson at openside and Tupou Vaa'i at blindside.

Ardie Savea scores a try against Ireland. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Codie Taylor is at hooker with Tyrel Lomax and Ethan de Groot the starting props.

There was plenty of speculation as to who would play lock and Rennie has gone with Fabian Holland and Josh Lord in the second row, with Vaa'i to provide cover.

In the backs, Roigard returns at halfback with Ruben Love at first-five and Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea in the midfield.

McKenzie has overcome the ankle injury that ruled him out of the win over the Bulls last weekend and will start at fullback, with Jordan and Josh Moorby on the wings.

Rennie has gone with a 5-3 split of forwards and backs on the bench, which includes front rowers Asafo Aumua, George Bower and Fletcher Newell, loose forwards Peter Lakai and Anton Segner, midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown, halfback Kyle Preston and outside back Leroy Carter.

Damian McKenzie celebrates a try with teammates. Photosport

Rennie said they can't wait to run out on Ellis Park on Sunday morning (NZT).

"After all the build up and anticipation, our whole touring squad is excited to get this first Test underway," Rennie said.

"We have selected a balanced mix of big match, experienced players and younger players who have earned the right to play in this first Test."

Rennie said the three games against the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls in South Africa have proved invaluable as they prepare for their biggest challenge of the year so far.

"The first three franchise games have exposed our newer players to the way South African teams play and have been fantastic in helping us build combinations and develop the game we want to play.

"We know the Test series will be a huge step up. We're well aware of what the Springboks will bring to the contest and the pressure that will come to bear. They are number one in the world, playing at their spiritual home in front of their passionate fans, so we will have to be at our very best on Saturday."

Josh Moorby in action against the Bulls. Photosport

Savea, Roigard and Jordan will make their first appearance of the tour in the match, while Savea and Taylor are playing their 110th Tests.

It will be Savea's 18th Test against South Africa and Taylor's 17th.

Segner and Moorby will be playing the Springboks for the first time.

World.title: Wellington residents march on Parliament in bid to get rising water bills lowered
World.content:
Hundreds gather in Wellington to protest new Tiaki Wai bills Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Some Wellington residents are fed up and stressed by the prospect of rising water bills as they marched on Parliament in a bid to get the organisation to lower costs.

And a former Wellington mayor-turned MP, who turned out to the protest, admitted his was among councils which could have invested more in water infrastructure in previous years.

About 300 people turned up in central Wellington on Thursday to raise concerns about their water bills in a cost of living crisis, as part of the Stop Tiaki Wai group.

Water bills are increasing by 13.3 percent on average across the region this year, and are projected to reach over $6000 per year in a decade.

A sign at Thursday's protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Lower Hutt resident AJ said that's shocking.

"The people are fed up, you can't get blood out of a stone can you?"

She said her first water bill was about $500 for the quarter.

"I came out here today, because the cost of living is through the roof, and this is just one more bill that people have to find money to pay - and people can't find that money anymore."

Mary Head, an Upper Hutt resident and pensioner, said she's frustrated about the way her water bills were being calculated.

"There's only my husband and I at home, and the amount of water we use, is negligible to say a family - and yet we are paying the same or more of a family of six or eight," she said.

Mary Head at the protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tiaki Wai said in its first years' of operation, the way water services would be calculated was taken from councils' rates bills.

In Upper Hutt, Porirua and Lower Hutt water bills were being calculated through a combination of a fixed rate and property value.

In Wellington city, most people's bills were based on property valuation, board chairperson Will Peet recently told RNZ.

The entity has said it wants to move to a single-pricing model in the future, as well as install water meters.

But Head said the indicative costs Tiaki Wai had put out for that so far - at half-a billion dollars for the programme - were ridiculous.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns admitted he couldn't actually stop Tiaki Wai - which was set up under the government's Local Water Done Well policy.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Nunns said he would be paying his bill this year - but suggested he would encourage people to not pay their bills if the costs didn't change.

That's not something Wellington City Councillor Karl Tiefenbacher, who was among the crowd at parliament, agreed with.

"I don't think that really works. To be fair I am against the fact we have no rates cap on top of Tiaki Wai - I think that's the issue."

He asked what the point of rates caps against councils were, if there was none against water entities.

"I think water is the biggest issue we have. I think this protest actually represents what is wrong with our society at the moment, and that's that it's becoming unaffordable."

When asked whether he thought spending was needed to upgrade failing pipes and water plants, Nunns said "no one" was happy with the current state of infrastructure.

Attendees at the protest on Thursday. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"We have always paid for water infrastructure in our rates, people have not necessarily understood that, they'll be understanding it now - but at $2200 a year, and until recently I was the sole occupant of the property, that's not realistic."

New Zealand First MP and former Wellington city councillor and mayor Andy Foster was also at the protest.

He was asked whether the council he led between 2019 and 2022 did enough to invest in pipes during its years in power.

He said his council set in motion more investment and was heading in the direction of a CCO for infrastructure, but also said more could have been done.

"We were going to fix it, so long term, yes, there was under-investment in infrastructure, but that is true of pretty-well every council in the country."

Tiaki Wai said it needed to spend $25 billion dollars across three decades to fix the regions old failing water treatment plants and pipes.

Stop Tiaki Wai protest attendee, Bridie McGill with her sign. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Officials said there's a major crisis point at Seaview, where a crucial outfall pipe was leaking into the harbour and the Waiwhetū stream.

They also said about 100 kilometres of pipe at the point needed to be replaced each year.

In a recent interview with RNZ, Tiaki Wai chief executive Michael Brewster urged anyone facing hardship to contact the organisation, saying Tiaki Wai had policies in place to help those who were really struggling to pay bills.

But he said debt collection would have to be pursued for those who were refusing to pay for no reason.

"If you are refusing to pay the bill and not contacting us then we, we would unfortunately, we would have to pursue that.

"Because at the end of the day there is an obligation to pay the bill, if nobody pays their bill we've got no money to fix the system."

Attendees march to Parliament. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said on Thursday, he respected the rights of Wellingtonians to join the protest and express their views.

But he urged the protesters to respect those working at Tiaki Wai trying to upgrade the region's infrastructure.

World.title: Former Tauranga mayor says he wasn't warned about landslide risk amid damning review
World.content:
A former mayor of Tauranga says warnings about the landslide risk on Mount Maunganui never reached him in his 12 years at the helm.

A damning review by former High Court judge Paul Davison KC found the council failed to act on several warnings over the course of 27 years about the risk of a slip on the nearby campground.

Stuart Crosby was mayor of Tauranga for 12 of those years, from 2004 to 2016.

"I watched online as Mr Davison gave his report, and to say it was confronting is an understatement," he said.

"Very disappointing in terms of the failure of processes within Tauranga City Council to get the right information to the right people to make the right decisions."

He said he hadn't been told about the slip risk.

"The areas that reached us were two, one was with regard to rockfall which we ... addressed, and the second was to put in fire prevention," he explained.

"Certainly to the best of my knowledge I don't remember receiving any information about mitigating landslips."

Former mayor says landslide risk warnings never reached him Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

He said it was a wake-up call for other councils.

"In fact, this morning I wrote an email to my own council, I'm on the Bay of Plenty Regional Council, requesting a report to go to our council with regard to information flow, and I'm sure this is happening up and down New Zealand," he said.

As for whether councils should look back through their records for any warnings they had missed, "I'm pretty sure they're doing it as we speak, I'm quite confident of that."

Dr Tom Robinson, a senior lecturer in disaster risk at the University of Canterbury, said the failings of Tauranga City Council weren't necessarily exclusive to it.

"What the report clearly shows is there are systematic errors, not just in Tauranga Council, that's the one that's been exposed here but those systematic problems that it's identified exist across the country," he said.

He echoed the sentiment that councils across New Zealand should consider the report a wake-up call.

"This is an opportunity for councils and organisations around the country to re-evaluate, look at some of the hazards and risks they're responsible for, and think about what actions they need to take," Robinson said.

"I think the problem, though, comes back to: councils have a huge amount of tasks and huge amounts of responsibilities, and dwindling reserves to be able to do that."

He said not enough money was spent on prevention.

"We've known for decades that a dollar spent on reduction reduces the amount you spend on response and recovery by 5, 7 or 10 dollars, you get the money back, and yet we're still putting the ambulance at the bottom of the hill and responding afterwards," he said.

World.title: Ombudsman shines light on 'coercive and unlawful treatment' at Wakari Hospital
World.content:
A Wakari Hospital patient with intellectual disabilities was almost constantly locked in their bedroom for at least 18 months in conditions the Chief Ombudsman says amounted to prolonged solitary confinement.

Inspectors for the Ombudsman visited the inpatient unit for adults with intellectual disabilities in Dunedin in March.

Last month, Chief Ombudsman John Allen shared the findings, saying inspectors observed some of the worst practices they had witnessed and some treatment amounted to torture.

Health New Zealand confirmed plans to close the ward on the same day, while the Ministry of Health said it would launch an independent investigation that would consider if allegations of human rights abuses should be referred to the police.

John Allen released a longer summary of the concerns and urgent recommendations on Thursday, detailing observations under the heading "punitive, coercive and unlawful treatment".

Inspectors detailed a model of care that appeared to prioritise containing and restricting patients to minimise the immediate risk of physical harm, with little attention given to providing meaningful rehabilitation or person-centred care, the report said.

The ward has faced significant criticism before, with a previous ombudsman calling it "a disgrace".

Dunedin's Wakari hospital inspected under crimes of torture Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

But the March inspection was triggered by an innocuous visit to check on a refurbishment Health New Zealand said would be underway from mid-2025, which would require patients to be relocated.

During an unannounced visit in October 2025, Ombudsman staff members discovered the refurbishment remained largely in the planning phase and patients had not been moved out.

They became "very concerned" about patients seen living in restrictive environments, flagging this with ward management and government agencies before sending an information request to Health New Zealand.

In December 2025, Health New Zealand confirmed a high level of restrictions remained at Ward 10A.

It prompted that four-day announced visit in March.

"We became very concerned about the conditions and treatment experienced by tāngata whaikaha (whaikaha means 'to have strength, to have ability, otherly abled, enabled')," the report said.

"We were concerned that the practices of the ward were extreme, fostered institutionalisation, risked traumatising tāngata whaikaha and may have constituted abuse."

Inspectors observed that one patient was locked in their bedroom "almost unceasingly" with extremely limited contact.

"We were very concerned that the physical arrangements were increasing the institutionalisation of this tāngata whaikaha, which had persisted for at least 18 months," the report said.

"We considered these arrangements may amount to prolonged solitary confinement."

The attempts to expose the patient to the ward also appeared to be very limited.

"At the time of the inspection, their bedroom door was being unlocked and left open for 90 seconds each day (rather than 30 seconds previously)," the report said.

The Ombudsman said it expected coercion was not used to modify behaviour and tāngata whaikaha had choice where possible.

Instead, the report outlined a pattern of staff incentivising good behaviour so patients could have their basics needs met including losing access to the toilet while in seclusion, being told they would only be able to see a dentist if their behaviour stabilised, or not being allowed to buy things with their own money unless they complied with staff directions.

"We were highly concerned about the potential use of punitive, coercive and unlawful practice on the ward."

Chief Ombudsman John Allen Supplied

Inspectors found patients might not have consented to some of the medication and sedatives they were given, including intramuscular injections.

This is not legal except in limited circumstances.

A bariatric EVAC mat was used to restrain and move patients, resulting in friction burns for some patients, despite the Ombudsman saying the United Nations' Special Rapporteur on Torture had raised concerns about the use of similar restraints and how they should only be used for legitimate medical reasons.

"In our view, moving a tangata whaikaha to a seclusion room is not a 'legitimate medical reason' envisaged by the Special Rapporteur," the report said.

Helensburgh Cottage, which was meant to help people to transition to care providers in the community, had remained empty since the pandemic despite the Ombudsman noting it appeared to be a better environment to provide care.

Staff told inspectors that it was not being used due to staffing pressures.

While detailing facts about Ward 10A, the Ombudsman noted that previous inspection reports found the physical environment was not fit for purpose - a description the former District Health Board also used.

The Ombudsman's concerns were detailed to senior staff at Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health after the visit, before urgent recommendations were made.

Allen did note that the relevant agencies had taken swift action in response to the concerns and recommendations.

The Ombudsman's recommendations included:

Health New Zealand urgently improving the "conditions of detention" by ending all prolonged isolation and improving physical living arrangements, activity and care.

Ending the use of bariatric EVAC mat to restrain and move tāngata whaikaha.

Urgently take measures to ensure the individual safety and rehabilitation of all tāngata whaikaha on Ward 10A.

The Ministry of Health making sure an independent investigation was undertaken.

Immediately reviewing the medications prescribed to tāngata whaikaha on Ward 10A, to ensure that all medication is lawfully prescribed and administered.

Immediately implementing a model of care in Ward 10A that focusses on tāngata whaikaha well-being and rehabilitation.

Health New Zealand previously said it was taking the allegations made by the Chief Ombudsman and others very seriously.

"We take patient safety and care very seriously and want to acknowledge the patients, their families, and our staff, all of whom we are supporting during this period of change," a spokesperson said.

"Our focus remains on ensuring the safety, dignity, and rights of the current patients, while strengthening oversight and reviewing practices."

Health New Zealand planned to undertake a wider review of forensic intellectual disability services nationally, and said it had already enhanced clinical oversight, reviewed patient care and rehabilitation plans, strengthened approaches to reducing seclusion, and strengthened governance arrangements.

World.title: National MP Greg Fleming breaks ranks, criticises Budget tax change
World.content:
A first-term National MP has criticised a tax change the government has introduced, saying a plan to cap the donation tax credit has "zero" logic.

Maungakiekie MP Greg Fleming said work was underway to "fix" the cap, but the minister responsible said that was not the case.

Fleming was speaking at a charity sector political hui in Wellington on Thursday, when he was asked about the logic behind the $100,000 donation cap limit.

"Zero," he responded. "I've no problems with being quoted publicly on saying I think it was an error."

At the Budget, the government made changes to the charity tax credit rules, which would mean no more tax credits once donors give more than $100,000 to charities.

Individuals could claim a third of their charitable donations back as a tax credit, as long as the value of their donations did not exceed a third of their annual total taxable income.

The $100,000 cap will affect about 350 donors when it is introduced next April, but they represent about 10 percent of donations claimed or about $103 million.

In a regulatory impact statement, the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) said the government spent about $350 million a year on tax credits.

IRD took the view that there was no conclusive evidence the credits actually lead to more giving, and that there was a risk of bad actors and misuse, such as those claiming the credit in advance of the funds being applied to charitable purposes or deriving a private benefit from the donations.

When the cap was announced in May, Revenue Minister Simon Watts said it would ensure the donation tax-credit scheme remained financially sustainable and would also limit tax-planning risks that arose when a donor made a gift to a charity they controlled themselves.

The charities sector has expressed concern that the cap may make would-be donors consider dialling back their donations at a time the sector was already struggling - a view Fleming appeared to agree with.

Fleming said he understood why the cap had been brought in, but there were a "myriad" ways to fix the misuse of donor-advised funds, without introducing a cap.

He said the cap was a "sledgehammer to crack a walnut" and further changes would be made.

"I'm advocating really, really hard for this and I can assure you that work is underway to to fix that," he said.

Watts said Fleming's comments were not correct and the government's position had not changed since the Budget.

"These changes resulted from IRD concerns that, in some cases, the tax credit was being misused for tax planning purposes," he said. "The change does not come into effect until 1 April 2027 and only affects donations over $100,000.

World.title: Nursing graduate applies for more than 100 jobs without success
World.content:
Nursing graduates who have applied for hundreds of jobs and have not found work say it's devastating to hear there's a shortage of nurses.

The nurse's union says Aotearoa's health system is falling into a deeper crisis, with emergency departments and wards bursting at the seams.

It follows revelations that Health New Zealand has hired just 54 full-time equivalent nurses in the past two years.

Nursing graduates struggle to find work while hospitals in crisis Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The situation is driving some graduates to consider making the move to Australia... joining their course mates who have already left.

After finishing hundreds of unpaid placement hours in Auckland, Megan completed her Bachelor of Nursing late last year.

In Aotearoa, new nurses have to apply for graduate positions, some do this through Te Whatu Ora's application system called ACE.

Others apply directly to private hospitals, community organisations and primary care.

But since graduating in March, Megan has applied for more than 100 nursing jobs and hasn't had any luck.

"I feel like I've failed, or there's something that I'm not showing in my application. I didn't realise it was going to be this hard to get a job."

Megan told Checkpoint she's getting by on the Jobseeker benefit while she continues to look for work.

If she can't find work soon, she's eyeing up Australia and said she may be forced to give up on nursing entirely.

"If I don't get a job I'm either likely going to have to re-study something else, or go into a completely different workforce.

"The running joke at the moment is that I become a flight attendant, which I don't really want to, but I've got to get a job somewhere."

Megan said it doesn't make sense how hard it is to find work because of reported shortages and staff burnout.

"We see constantly that the hospitals are understaffed and people are dying.

"Going into an election year, how can you promise us as nurses, new grads and even the public that the hospitals are going to be staffed?"

Hearing stories of graduates not being able to get work has students worried too.

Eden Sandhu is in her final year of studying nursing at Ara Institute of Canterbury.

But seeing nurses the year above missing out on jobs has made her anxious.

"Like thinking that there's no guarantee of securing a graduate position is just draining.

"We're told that there's a shortage, but all of us still experience anxiety that people aren't getting jobs, will there be a position for me when I graduate?"

To get their degrees, nurses have to complete hundreds of hours of on-the-job training, which is not paid.

Eden Sandhu said she had sacrificed so much financially to become qualified and worried about the future.

"[It's] a huge a worry because I've got a family and a mortgage... it's not okay to have graduates coming through having to consider after three years, to find something else."

Moving to Australia is something that's been on Eden's mind over the past few months.

"I think if New Zealand focused on supporting the students through placement, offering paid placements, upping the amount nurses are paid for the incredible stress levels they carry.

"Focussing on how to keep nurses here and not have such a terrible environment that people need to shoot off, that would change how I feel about leaving," she said.

"I would want to stay, I do want to stay, but unfortunately [if I don't find a job] I can't."

Dawn Blyth, the Nurses Organisation's National Student Unit co-leader, is also in her final year of study.

People in her cohort have already applied to Australia's graduate programmes.

"I graduate in November... we understand that jobs aren't guaranteed anywhere in any climate.

"But what is really hard to understand is how can we be saying that our country is so short of nurses... when there isn't the funds to put those nurses into jobs."

Health New Zealand national chief nurse Nadine Gray told Checkpoint they were offering a similar number of roles to last year to keep a mix of experienced and graduate nurses.

She said they were supporting all graduate registered nurses into employment, but this might not happen immediately, and they had never been able to employ every graduate nurse.

World.title: Former Alliance candidate Mary O’Neill sentenced for harassment of Napier neighbours
World.content:
A former local government and parliamentary candidate has been warned she could end up in prison if she does not stop harassing her neighbours.

Mary Jelena O'Neill, 62, was sentenced in the Napier District Court on Thursday for a single charge of intentional damage.

The offending happened in Napier, but O'Neill appeared via an audio-visual link from Dunedin, where she now lives.

The charge, which was proven against her at a judge-alone trial this year, was laid after O'Neill hired a contractor to cut back trees on the property of her neighbours on Napier's Bluff Hill.

However, Judge Russell Collins said the heart of the matter was not the physical damage caused but a "cynical act of harassment" towards the neighbours.

O'Neill has a previous history of harassing the same neighbours - including four breaches of a protection order in 2021 - and other people, dating back to a charge of threatening behaviour in 2015.

Court documents from 2021 say she made "false and damaging" accusations of sexual misconduct about one of her neighbours to the authorities and on social media.

She also once threw a rock at an AA serviceman who had been called out to fix a neighbour's car, then drove towards him, stopping about 60cm away.

Judge Collins stopped short of imposing a custodial sentence on O'Neill, saying she had "complex needs" and her claims about the neighbouring family were "delusional".

Instead, he imposed a maximum term of two years of intensive supervision by a probation officer.

The supervision includes conditions that O'Neill lives at the Dunedin address and does not go near her former house or neighbour's house on Napier Hill.

She will also need to do any counselling thought necessary.

She is not allowed to contact her victims or post anything about them on social media.

Judge Collins warned O'Neill that if she breached her intensive supervision, or reoffended, "I doubt that you would avoid a term of imprisonment", or at least an electronically monitored sentence such as home detention.

O'Neill stood unsuccessfully as a candidate in the Hawke's Bay Regional Council elections in 2019 under the name Jelena Jordan.

She was previously an Alliance Party candidate for Parliament in 2011 and 2014.

This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Woman and child seriously assaulted during Northland break in, man arrested
World.content:
A woman and her child were injured in an assaulted during an alleged break in at a Northland property.

Police have arrested a 38-year-old man following what they called a "violent aggravated robbery" in Kaikohe at 7am on Thursday.

Detective Senior Sergeant Aaron Crawford said police were called to a report of a man allegedly carrying a gun, breaking into a property on Williams St.

A woman and her child were inside, Crawford said, and the pair were "seriously assaulted" before a man fled in a car he stole from the home.

The police Eagle helicopter found the car a short time later in Ōmāpere.

Crawford said the man police believed was involved attempted to run and allegedly tried to steal another car by assaulting another person.

Police intervened, Crawford said, and took him into custody.

A gun and items police believed belonged to the home of the woman and child had since been found, he said.

The woman was taken to hospital in a serious but stable condition, Crawford said, and the child had minor injuries.

"Both are understandably shaken," he said.

The 38-year-old man was in custody and Crawford said charges were pending.

Police wanted to hear from anyone who saw what happened on Williams St or any sightings of a yellow Suzuki Swift travelling west on SH12 towards Whirinaki, Kouto Loop Rd and then Opononi and Ōmāpere.

They also wanted to hear from anyone who saw a man acting "suspiciously" in the Ōmāpere area on Thursday morning.

Information could be provided online at 105.police.govt.nz, or by calling 105 and using the reference number 260820/5258.

World.title: Max Verstappen signs to stay with Red Bull F1
World.content:
Max Verstappen has ended speculation over his Formula 1 future by signing a contract extension that will see him remain at Red Bull Racing until 2030.

The four-time world champion has repeatedly threatened to walk away from F1 this season in protest at the new power unit in use.

Red Bull have struggled with the regulations this year, with Verstappen's best performances two second-place finishes in Austria and Hungary.

Verstappen sits in sixth place in the drivers' standings this season without a win through the first 11 grands prix.

The Dutch star, who finished just two points behind world champion Lando Norris last season, was previously contracted to the end of 2028.

However, there were clauses in his contract that could have allowed him to leave at the end of the season.

The Red Bull team have struggled under the new regulations. (Getty Images: PA Images/David Davies)

The 28-year-old was linked with potential moves to Mercedes and McLaren, involving an outlandish driver swap with Australian Oscar Piastri; however, he will now stay at the team with whom he has won 71 grands prix.

"I am really pleased with the contract extension," Verstappen said in a statement.

"We have the best people, and I'm excited to keep working together with everyone to get back to the top again.

"This remains the ultimate goal that all of us have been working towards and will continue to pursue. I want to thank Red Bull, Laurent [Mekies] and everyone at Oracle Red Bull Racing for the trust they put in me."

The F1 season has just finished its summer break, with racing to resume at Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix this weekend at Zandvoort, the last time the circuit will be on the calendar.

"To make this announcement during the last Grand Prix at Zandvoort is a great moment for me as well," Verstappen said.

"Hopefully we can give the fans a special send-off for the final race."

Verstappen won the first two Dutch Grand Prix upon the race's return to F1 in 2021, but has been beaten into second place the last two seasons, by Norris in 2024 and Piastri last season.

"I have always said it, the team is like a second family for me, and I feel very at home," Verstappen said.

"I came to the team hoping to be able to win races. What we went on to achieve together has been simply lovely.

"To continue this journey with the same team that I have been with my whole career is really special and something I have always wanted to do."

Max Verstappen will be racing in F1 until 2030 after signing a new contract. (Getty Images: Marcel van Dorst/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto)

Verstappen joined the Red Bull Junior Programme in 2014 and, after starting 23 grands prix for Scuderia Toro Rosso, made his F1 debut with the full Red Bull team midway through the 2016 season as a replacement for Daniil Kvyat.

The then-teenage star claimed a stunning victory in that race, becoming the youngest-ever grand prix winner aged 18 years and 228 days.

"Having Max continue with us and retaining the best driver on the grid is fantastic news for everyone at Red Bull, Oracle Red Bull Racing, as well as F1 and motorsport as a whole," Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said.

"Very few partnerships in sport achieve what Max and this team have.

"His impact on our team and on Red Bull's motorsport story has been transformational, and he has been fundamental to everything we have accomplished together.

"But we are not done yet. There are more races to win, more milestones to achieve and more history to write."

Red Bull has already had to deal with some disruption in the mid-season shutdown, with Isack Hadjar suffering a wrist injury that will rule him out of the Dutch Grand Prix.

New Zealander Liam Lawson will step up and take Hadjar's seat, with test driver Yuki Tsunoda taking the Kiwi's Racing Bulls seat for the round.

World.title: Swans sponsors pull support in wake of allegations
World.content:
A number of brands associated with the Sydney Swans have suspended their activities with the club in the wake of a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault in Melbourne on Monday.

Five Swans players, Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon are linked to the police investigation.

The players are yet to be formally interviewed or charged and it is not suggested that any of them are being accused of sexual assault.

Sponsors Colgate, Volkswagen and Telstra have confirmed to the ABC that they have "suspended" or "paused" their activities with the players involved.

Other sponsors, including QBE and realestate.com.au, have released statements condemning any abuse or violence against women but have stopped short of withdrawing their support for the club.

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich expressed a "sincere apology for the distress this incident has caused the wider community," in a statement released on Wednesday afternoon, naming "members, supporters, commercial partners, Academy families, staff members, athletes, their partners and families".

'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident Five Sydney Swans players stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards issue an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

"Our thoughts remain with everyone affected, particularly the women involved. All women deserve to feel safe and respected," the statement read.

"We understand and share the hurt that many of you we will be feeling. To say we are disappointed is an understatement.

"We know that moving forward as a club will take time.

"Every member of our community will process this in their own way, and we do not take your trust or support for granted.

"We are committed to doing the work required to uphold the values, standards and culture we expect of everyone at the Sydney Swans."

Andrew Pridham (right) and Matthew Pavlich have apologised to parties affected by the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

A number of club sponsors have expressed concerns, but added that they would not comment on the matter while the police investigation was ongoing.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson told the ABC.
